Start here

The till held. What sat behind it did not.

September 2026 banked ₹15,29,410 across 213 transactions — a fall of just 2.3% on September 2025 and, read on its own, an unremarkable month. The average sale actually rose, from ₹7,178 to ₹7,180, and the median sale rose from ₹1,770 to ₹1,942. On the headline numbers this is a steady month.

Three things underneath it are not steady, and they are what this report is about.

The one-line version, if you read nothing else. The studio served 394 members this September against 305 last September — its widest September base in three years — and collected ₹3,316 of class revenue from each of them against ₹3,218. Both of those went up. The only thing that went down is how often each of them came: 3.56 visits against 4.84. That single change is worth more than the entire year-on-year movement in the cash line, and it is the difference between a studio running at capacity and one running at 42.6%.

First, the month was funded by people the studio already had. Members making their first-ever Bandra purchase contributed ₹3,00,229, or 19.6% of the month; existing members contributed the other ₹12,29,182. That is normal for a mature studio, and it is genuinely good news about the base. It also means September’s cash figure tells you almost nothing about September’s acquisition performance. The two must be read separately.

A note on that number: 19.6% counts members whose first purchase at Bandra was in September. The performance review quotes 12.5% on a different and narrower definition — clients whose first visit was in September, who paid a narrower sum. The two measures diverge because some September visitors had already bought a package, and some September buyers had already visited. Both are correct; the purchase-based figure is the relevant one for a sales report.

Second, the commitment length is shortening. Three-month memberships sold 18 units in April 2025 and 2 in September 2026. One-month memberships fell from 29 units to 15 over the same year. The products that give the studio a forward revenue cushion are being sold less often than they were.

Third — and this is the finding with the most consequence — the studio is now selling almost exactly what it delivers. In September 2024, ₹23,96,991 of cash translated into ₹7,73,072 of attended classes: 32%. In September 2025 that rose to 63%. In September 2026 it reached 85%. That is a profound structural change and it deserves to be named plainly, because it cuts both ways.

The same flat top line means something completely different in 2026 than it did in 2024

Two years ago a large share of the cash the studio took was never drawn down as classes. Members bought packages and long memberships, attended less than they paid for, and the studio kept the difference. That unused capacity was quiet, real revenue — and it was also a symptom of disengagement.

By September 2026 that cushion has largely gone: 85 of every ₹100 banked is now delivered as an attended class, against 32 two years earlier. The studio is selling shorter, cheaper, more-consumable products to members who use them. The revenue is more honest. It is also more fragile, because the same flat cash figure now has to be earned every month rather than partly collected in advance.

This is the single most useful reframe in the report. Bandra’s September problem is not that revenue collapsed — it did not. It is that the business model quietly shifted from selling commitment to selling consumption, while the cash total stayed flat and therefore hid the change. Everything the studio needs to fix about retention now has a shorter runway than it did, because there is far less prepaid, unused membership to absorb a bad month.

The base is widening

More people came to Bandra this September than in either of the last two. They each came less often.

This is the finding that reframes the whole month. The cash line fell 2.3%, and it is tempting to read that as demand weakening. The check-in ledger says the opposite: 394 individual members trained at Bandra in September 2026, against 305 in September 2025 and 355 in September 2024 — a base that has grown 29% year on year. The studio is reaching more people than it ever has in a September.

What fell was frequency. The average member trained 3.56 times in September 2026 against 4.84 times a year earlier. Revenue per active member went the other way — ₹3,316 against ₹3,218, up 3.0%. Each member is worth more; there are just fewer visits in each of them. Fewer seats were sold, but they were better-paid seats.

The loyal core halved its frequency

Seventy-eight people who trained here last September came back this September. Between them they gave the studio 252 fewer visits.

This is treated in full in the class performance report, because it is fundamentally a question of volume rather than of money. Its cash consequence is easy to state, though. The 252 visits those members did not make are, at September’s class revenue of ₹931 a head, roughly ₹2,34,491 of class revenue the studio never booked — in a month when the entire cash line moved by ₹35,322. Frequency, not price, is where the money went.

A membership business has two jobs: get paid, and get the member to re-commit. The second job is the one that compounds. Bandra’s membership line is being held up by one-month products while the longer commitments — the ones that roll over less often and generate far more lifetime value per conversation — shrink to almost nothing.

Three-month memberships are the clearest case: 18 units in April 2025, 2 units in September 2026. In the same window one-month units fell from 29 to 15. Only the new six-month and annual tiers grew, and from a base of almost zero. This is a sales-mix problem, not a demand problem — the members are still buying; they are buying shorter.

Why this matters more than the flat top line suggests

A one-month member makes twelve purchase decisions a year. A three-month member makes four. A twelve-month member makes one. Every step down in commitment length multiplies the number of moments at which the studio can lose the member — and the data shows September losing them in exactly those moments. Combined with a delivery ratio that has risen from 32% to 85%, the studio now has both a shorter commitment base and less prepaid cushion to absorb the consequences.

The ladder is mostly rational: per-class cost falls as the package grows, from ₹1,943 for a single class to ₹1,444 inside the 12-class pack. Two rungs break the pattern, and both are worth acting on.

The 10-class package at ₹1,735 a class is priced above the 12-class pack while selling for essentially the same money — an average ticket of ₹17,350 against ₹17,325. Thirteen members bought the worse-value option in September. And the 2-for-1 intro pack halves the price again to ₹971 a class, which is defensible as acquisition but sets the member’s price expectation extremely low at exactly the moment they are deciding whether the studio is worth full price.

Discounting is disciplined in volume and loose in depth. Only 36 of 213 sales carried a discount, but the depth averaged 15.0% and reached 19.2% on the annual membership and the 20-class pack, against 14.4% on the standard monthly and three-month products. The deeper discounts sit on the highest-value products — which is where each percentage point costs the most. The annual membership’s discount alone was ₹41,800.

How the money arrived

Online payments now carry the largest tickets by a factor of two, and discounting is almost entirely code-driven.

Four channels took the month’s money. Counter and custom payment took the most transactions — 151 sales worth ₹8,92,920 — but the largest average ticket sits with Stripe at ₹12,820 on 28 sales, more than twice the cash average of ₹4,780. The pattern is not incidental: the products that require a decision — annual and six-month memberships, multi-class packs — are bought on cards and online, while day-to-day singles are bought at the desk. Stripe transactions fell from 53 to 28 year on year; multi-method sales, where a member splits a large purchase, doubled from 6 to 13.

Discounting is concentrated in five codes, and three of them are acquisition codes rather than retention codes. Two codes alone — NC-2026-SHQ (20 uses, ₹61,129 given away) and ZAP10 (14 uses, ₹53,380) — account for ₹1,14,509 of the ₹1,63,709 given away. A single use of the 20OFFSHQ code cost ₹41,800 on its own. Because a code requires intent, every rupee of discount here is a rupee someone asked for and was granted — which makes it a policy question, not a leakage question.

Who the money came from

Ten members account for more than a third of the month. Half of all buyers account for seven per cent.

September’s 139 paying members are not a flat distribution. The top ten by spend account for 38% of the month’s cash, the top twenty for 52%, while the bottom half of buyers contribute 7.3%. That is not unusual for a boutique studio and it is not a problem — but it does mean that two or three decisions by high-value members move the monthly number more than any campaign aimed at the base. The single largest purchase of the month, an annual unlimited membership at ₹1,75,560, was worth more than the combined purchases of the bottom 48 buyers.

The other side of concentration is breadth of need. 83% of September buyers bought from only one product category. Only 23 of 139 members bought across two categories, and a single member bought across four. There is very little cross-selling happening: a member who joins for Barre and a member who joins for PowerCycle are, on this month’s evidence, treated as the same customer until they leave.

What the first purchase predicts

Nothing in the sales ledger separates members as sharply as the product they started on — except how quickly they came back.

Take the 4,218 people whose first visit to Bandra is on record and group them by the first thing they bought. The spread in eventual lifetime value is not marginal, it is structural. A member who started on a 1 Month Unlimited is worth ₹74,283 to the studio. One who started on a Single Class is worth ₹13,689. Between them sit every other product in the range, in a consistent order: memberships first, packages second, single classes last.

The obvious caution applies, and it is worth stating plainly: members who chose a bigger commitment were already more committed. But the gap is 5.4-fold, and the studio sells both products from the same front desk within the same minute. What a new client is offered first is not a neutral choice.

The second predictor is time, and it is even more directly actionable. Of every first-timer on record, the speed at which they took a second class divides their eventual value almost as sharply as their first purchase did. Members who returned within a week are worth ₹27,745 on average; those who took a month, or never came back at all, are worth ₹13,918.

Recommendations

Thirteen actions, ordered by expected value

The first three protect what already works. Four are pricing and structure. The last four attack frequency, channel and cross-selling — the levers that do not require a single new customer. Each recommendation carries the reasoning behind it and the impact the studio should expect, so it can be argued with rather than simply accepted.

01

Re-weight the product ladder toward 12-class packages

Sales + Studio Manager

ReasoningThe 12-class package sells at ₹1,444 a class — the best value the studio offers — and it grew +₹68,740 on four more sales. The 10-class package costs the member ₹1,735 a class and sold 13 units at almost exactly the same average ticket. Both price at roughly ₹17,300. A member choosing the 10-class package over the 12 is paying the same money for two fewer classes.

Expected impactMoving 6 of September’s 13 ten-class sales up to the twelve-class tier adds 12 class credits to the studio’s delivered base at no revenue cost, and is the cleanest available improvement to the entry offer. On September volume that is worth about ₹1.1 lakh of delivered capacity a year.

02

Put a named owner on every repeat sale

Studio Manager

Reasoning41 of September’s 139 paying members bought more than once — and they produced 34.1% of the month’s ₹15,29,410. Meanwhile ₹3,66,511 of September sales — 24% — have no salesperson recorded, the largest single block in the ledger.

Expected impactNamed attribution on the unattributed block would make the repeat-purchase cycle visible and manageable for the first time. Selling one additional package to each of the 98 single-purchase members at September’s median ticket of ₹1,942 is worth roughly ₹1.9 lakh a month.

03

Fix the three-month membership before it disappears

Sales + Finance

ReasoningThree-month memberships ran at 18 units in April 2025 and 2 units in September 2026. Over the same period one-month units fell from 29 to 15. Long-duration commitments — the product that produces the studio’s cash cushion — are being sold less often in every length except the new annual tier.

Expected impactRecovering even 8 three-month units a month at the historic average ticket of about ₹24,900 returns roughly ₹24 lakh a year of higher-commitment revenue, and materially improves the deferred-revenue position.

04

Standardise discount depth at 15% and stop it leaking past it

Finance + Front Desk

Reasoning36 September transactions carried a discount worth ₹1,63,709 in total — 9.7% of list value. Depth averages 15.0%, but the annual membership was discounted 19.2% and the 20-class pack 19.2%, against 14.4% on the standard packages.

Expected impactHolding every discount to the 15% standard while keeping the same volume saves roughly ₹1.1 lakh a year on September’s pattern alone. Depth discipline is also the single easiest lever to audit.

05

Treat the single-class price as a deliberate tier, not a default

Sales

ReasoningSingle classes at ₹1,943 each are now the second-largest unit line at 38 sales, up +₹20,799 year on year. They are profitable per head but they never build a habit, and ₹1,943 a class is the worst value the member can pick.

Expected impactConverting a third of September’s 38 single-class buyers into a four-class package at the point of purchase adds about ₹56,000 of committed revenue from the same people, and gives them a reason to return.

06

Protect the new long-duration products

Sales + Finance

ReasoningSeptember produced the studio’s first ₹1,75,560 annual membership and a ₹1,02,344 six-month sale — together ₹2,77,904, or 18.2% of the month, from two transactions. Both are new propositions and neither existed in September 2025.

Expected impactAn annual and a six-month sale replace roughly 15 one-month renewals. If these two products can be sold four times a month rather than once, they add about ₹11 lakh a year while lengthening the average commitment.

07

Make the 213 sales count for retention, not just cash

CRM

Reasoning139 members paid the studio in September, against 143 new clients acquired. The two numbers are close, which means the month’s acquisition effort is not yet compounding into the paying base — and the existing base contributed 80.4% of the ₹15,29,410.

Expected impactEvery September buyer who is not booked into a class within 14 days is a renewal risk. A checkout prompt to book the next class is the cheapest retention intervention available and costs nothing to build.

08

Attack frequency, not price — the money is in the fourth visit

Studio Manager + CRM

ReasoningThe check-in ledger shows the base widening to 394 members while visits per member fell to 3.56 from 4.84. In the same ledger, members who trained in both Septembers cut their own frequency 35%, costing 252 visits — 18% of everything filled this month. Cash per member actually rose, from ₹3,218 to ₹3,316.

Expected impactThis is the only lever in the report that does not require new customers. Lifting the 98 members who came exactly once this month to two visits would add about 98 attendances — roughly ₹91,238 — without a single rupee of acquisition spend.

09

Make the online checkout the default for every membership

Sales + Finance

ReasoningStripe sales averaged ₹12,820 a transaction against ₹4,780 for cash, and split-payment sales averaged ₹13,628. Stripe transactions fell from 53 to 28 year on year while counter sales rose. The high-value products are migrating off the channel that handles them best.

Expected impactRouting every membership and multi-class pack through a card-on-file or link-based checkout removes the desk as a bottleneck for the products that need a considered decision, and makes the second purchase a one-tap action rather than a visit.

10

Put all discount codes under one owner

Finance

ReasoningTwo codes — NC-2026-SHQ and ZAP10 — account for ₹1,14,509 of the ₹1,63,709 given away in September, on 34 of the month’s 213 sales. A further single use of 20OFFSHQ cost ₹41,800. Meanwhile the unattributed salesperson block carried the deepest average discount of any channel at 14.8%, against 5.6% for Imran Shaikh.

Expected impactCodes are created by whoever needs one, and nobody compares them. One owner, one register, one monthly review of depth by code makes the discount line controllable for the first time and would have caught the 20OFFSHQ depth before it was granted.

11

Sell the second category

Studio Manager

Reasoning83% of September buyers bought from a single product category and only 23 of 139 shopped across two. The top ten buyers produced 38% of the month’s cash while the bottom half produced 7.3%. A boutique studio lives on the second and third purchase, not the first.

Expected impactA single bundle — one Barre class, one Cycle class, priced to be obviously better than either alone — is the cheapest way to move members out of a single format. Members who train in two formats are the studio’s most durable customers, and on this month’s data almost nobody is being asked to become one.

12

Lead with the membership, not the single class

Sales + Front Desk

ReasoningA first-time buyer who starts on a 1 Month Unlimited goes on to be worth ₹74,283; one who starts on a Single Class is worth ₹13,689. There are 200 people in that bottom group and 172 in the top one.

Expected impactBoth are sold at the same desk. Presenting the commitment first — and treating the trial entry as a route into it rather than as a purchase in its own right — changes the mix without touching the price list.

13

Book the second class before the first one ends

Front Desk + Sales + CRM

ReasoningMembers who took their second class inside a week are worth ₹27,745; those who waited a month or never returned are worth ₹13,918. There are 401 people in that last group alone.

Expected impactThis is a front-desk action, not a campaign: at the end of every first class, before the client leaves the building, the next visit is chosen and booked. It costs nothing, it is measurable within a week, and on this data it is the highest-value habit the sales and service teams could adopt.

Method and limitations

How to read these numbers, and what they cannot show

Sources and method

Three exports at a snapshot of 11 October 2026. Sales – Raw (25,044 succeeded payments network-wide, 6,547 at Bandra) provides cash received, product, discount, salesperson and payment method. Day End Report – Part 3 – Sessions (25,675 class occurrences) provides revenue attributed to attended classes. Day End Report – Part 1 – New (21,171 member records) identifies which September revenue came from clients acquired that month.

What the two revenue measures mean, and why both are shown

Cash is money actually received on a payment date; it is what the studio banked. Class-attributed revenue is what the platform allocates to each attended class; it is what the studio delivered. They are different numbers on purpose, and the gap between them is the most informative thing in this report — it measures how much of what members paid for has not yet been consumed. A widening gap means members are holding unused credits; a narrowing gap means the studio is selling closer to what it delivers.

Known limitations

  • No cost of sale. No CAC, contribution margin or payroll cost is present in this data, so payback and profitability cannot be calculated. All figures are gross value.
  • Salesperson cover. 24% of September revenue has no salesperson recorded. Attributed performance is therefore a floor on each named seller, not a full picture.
  • Retail is understated in scope. Retail appears here as a revenue line only; no stock, cost or sell-through data is available.
  • Comparability. September 2025 followed Ganesh Chaturthi (27 August); September 2026 absorbed it (14 September). Single-month year-on-year comparisons carry that distortion. The year-to-date table is the more reliable frame.

This report sets that against the 1,889 seats that went unused, and shows that they are concentrated in specific formats, days and hours that the studio controls. The numbers behind the number: 78 members trained here in both Septembers — the same people, twelve months apart. They made 713 visits last September and 461 this one, a fall of 35.3% and a shortfall of 252 attendances. Acquisition is working. Start here

The classes got better. There are simply fewer good ones than there should be.

Class performance is the one part of Bandra’s September that improved on nearly every measure, and it deserves to be said clearly before the problems. The studio ran 259 classes against 273 a year earlier — a leaner timetable — and filled 42.6% of the seats against 41.8%. Revenue attributed to attended classes rose from ₹9,81,453 to ₹13,06,451, up 33%, making it the only revenue line in the studio that grew. Revenue per class rose 40% to ₹5,044; revenue per attendee rose from ₹665 to ₹931. Late cancellations fell from 658 to 199.

Every one of those is a genuine operational gain, and two Septembers of improvement in a row — from 27.3% in 2024 to 41.8% to 42.6% — is a trend rather than noise.

What the same numbers also show is a large and specific inefficiency that has been carried for three years without being addressed. The studio holds a fixed-cost timetable and fills just over two seats in five. In September 2026 it offered 3,293 seats and used 1,404 of them. The unused 1,889 seats are not evenly spread: they are concentrated in particular formats, particular days and particular hours, and the concentration is stable enough across two years to be treated as a design flaw rather than a bad month.

The single most useful sentence in this report is this: Studio PowerCycle runs 35% of the timetable and fills 35.0% of it, while Studio FIT runs 15% of the timetable and fills 71.0%. Both are good products with loyal followings. Only one of them is being given the right amount of the week.

And a fourth finding, which is new in this edition and changes what the first three mean. The studio is not short of people. 394 members trained here in September 2026 against 305 a year earlier — a wider base than in either of the last two Septembers. What fell was how often they came: 3.56 visits each against 4.84. The 78 members who were here in both Septembers cut their own frequency 35%, and those missing 252 visits are 18% of everything the studio filled this month. The room is not emptying because people stopped coming. It is emptying because the people who come are coming less.

The loyal core halved its frequency

Seventy-eight people who trained here last September came back this September. Between them they gave the studio 252 fewer visits.

78 members trained at Bandra in both September 2025 and September 2026. This is a true like-for-like group — same people, same month, twelve months apart. In September 2025 they made 713 visits (9.14 each). In September 2026 they made 461 (5.91 each). That is a fall of 35.3% in the frequency of the studio’s most committed customers.

The arithmetic matters more than the percentage. Those 252 lost visits are 18% of every seat that was filled in September 2026. Had the core held its year-ago frequency, September 2026 would have recorded 1,656 attendances — ahead of September 2025’s 1,476, not behind it. The month’s decline is not an acquisition failure at all. It is a frequency failure among people who already know the studio.

Only members with at least one attended visit in both months are counted, so no joining or leaving distorts the comparison. The 2025–26 pair is a smaller and more committed group by construction, which makes its 35% decline more notable, not less.

Nobody was lost. Nothing was converted.

The churn is almost entirely people who came once and never came back — and it is being replaced in volume.

Of the 227 members who trained in September 2025 and did not appear in September 2026, 126 had made exactly one visit in that month, and 105 of the 227 were last seen in September 2025 itself. On lifetime numbers the distinction is stark: the members who stayed had averaged 161 career visits, while the ones who left averaged 34. The studio is not losing its regulars. It is failing to convert its trials.

And the replacements are working harder than the departures did. The 316 members who had no September 2025 visit delivered 943 attendances this month; the 227 who left behind them had delivered only 763 a year ago. New blood out-performed old losses by 24%. The problem is not that the studio cannot recruit. It is that it recruits at the top of the funnel and leaks at the bottom.

What the booking book says

Bookings fell four times faster than attendance. That is the cleanest warning in the data.

Attendance is a lagging number — it tells you what happened in the room. The booking book tells you what members intended to do, and it moved sharply. Members booked 2,134 seats in September 2025 and 1,604 in September 2026, a fall of 25%. Attendance fell only 4.9%. The two numbers have come apart, and the gap is entirely explained by discipline: 658 late cancellations became 199.

Two things are true at once. The studio is now far better at converting an intention into a visit — 69.2% of booked seats were actually used a year ago, against 87.5% now, and revenue per booked seat rose from ₹460 to ₹814. But the intention pool itself is drying up: the book now covers only 48.7% of the seats on the board, down from 60.5%. Tightening cancellation policy has improved the conversion of demand that already exists. It has not created any new demand.

Why this matters more than the fill rate

Fill rate is computed after the fact. Bookings are the leading indicator, and the book is now half-empty 48.7% of capacity was ever claimed. A timetable designed for 3,293 seat-slots is being asked to serve a book of 1,604. Until the booking rate rises, no amount of scheduling refinement will fill the room — there is nothing left to convert.

The room is bigger than the demand

Small rooms fill. Large rooms do not. The studio has been quietly fixing this — and has further to go.

Sort the month’s sessions by how many seats the room holds and a clean pattern appears. Rooms of ten and eleven seats ran 62.4% full across 62 sessions. Rooms of twelve and thirteen ran 37.3% across 99 sessions, and rooms of fourteen or more ran 38.5% across 98. The same pattern held a year earlier, so this is a property of the timetable, not of September.

The encouraging part is that the studio has already begun to move. September 2025 ran 49 sessions in ten-to-eleven-seat rooms; September 2026 ran 62. Sessions in the largest rooms fell from 122 to 98. Shifting a class into a smaller room does not change how many people come — it changes how full the room looks and how much the same demand is worth, and revenue per session in the small-room band was ₹6,385 against ₹4,622 elsewhere.

16 per cent of the room was free

Complimentary seats rose by more than half while paid attendance fell. Barre 57 is the most affected.

Of the 1,404 attendances recorded in September 2026, 225 carried no payment — 16.0% of the room, against 9.7% a year earlier. Complimentary seats rose 57% while paid seats fell. Comps are not wrong in themselves: staff visits, partner classes and make-goods are legitimate. But they are invisible in an attendance-only report, and at this scale they change the meaning of the fill rate. A 42.6% fill on 3,293 seats is 1,404 attendances; 225 of them produced no revenue at all.

Studio Barre 57 is the format most affected: 27 of its 331 attendances (27%) were complimentary, against 4.0% for Studio FIT. The two hosted classes in the month — the Physique 57 partner sessions on 13 and 23 September — were 100% complimentary, 24 seats, zero revenue, and are correctly recorded as marketing rather than trading.

Who a first class brings in — and whether they come back

The day, hour and format of somebody’s very first class predicts their lifetime with unusual accuracy.

Take every member whose first ever Bandra class fell from January 2025 onward, follow them for their whole history, and split by the circumstances of that first visit. The differences are large enough to schedule against.

By day: people whose first class was on a Tuesday reach a third visit 32.0% of the time; those who started on a Sunday, 14.6%. By hour: a first class before 9am converts to a third visit 27.8% of the time and yields 9.5 visits on average, against 15.9% and 5.0 visits for an afternoon start. By format: a first class in Studio Barre 57 leads to a third visit 28.3% of the time and 8.4 visits, while a first class in Studio Mat 57 leads to 11.6% and 2.5 visits.

None of this means a Tuesday class is better than a Sunday class. It means that the people willing to start on a Tuesday, or before work, or in the Barre room, are a different kind of customer. The studio currently gives trials and first-timers to whichever slot has room. Utilisation falls from 47.7% in the first week of September to 41.8% in the fourth, while the number of sessions run falls only slightly. September 2025 followed the same shape, from 51.5% to 34.3%. Two consecutive years of the same arc means this is not an event, a festival or a marketing failure — it is the studio’s booking rhythm.

The likely mechanism is straightforward: members front-load their bookings when a new month or a new package cycle begins, and the final week runs on residual commitment. Whatever the cause, the shape is predictable, and a predictable dip is a schedulable one.

How the room pays for itself

The payment mix behind each format

This is the most strategically useful table in the report, because it shows which formats are doing acquisition work and which are doing retention work.

Studio PowerCycle is the studio’s trial engine. 8% of its attendance arrives on an intro offer, the highest of any format, and 14% buys in single classes. That is what an entry-point format looks like. Studio FIT is where members end up: 75% of its attendance is on memberships and only 1% on intro offers.

Read alongside the utilisation figures, that pairing explains the whole timetable problem. The studio is putting its lowest-intent traffic — trials and drop-ins — into its largest block of scheduled capacity, and reserving its best-performing format for a much smaller share of the week. The formats are not competing; they are mis-sequenced.

Recommendations

Fourteen actions, ordered by expected value

The first four are timetable decisions that cost nothing and can be made before next month’s schedule is published. The rest build the measurement and conversion discipline that would keep the improvements.

01

Right-size Studio PowerCycle

Programming + Studio Manager

ReasoningPowerCycle runs 90 sessions — 35% of the entire timetable — and fills 35.0% of its seats, down 8.8 points on last September. It is the only major format whose utilisation fell, and it absorbed 48 fewer attendees than a year ago. Meanwhile its capacity per class is 13.0 seats against an average attendance of 4.56.

Expected impactCutting PowerCycle’s average class size from 13 to 10 seats frees roughly 270 seat-hours a month without touching the timetable, and removes 8 empty sessions from the board. Raising its fill to Studio FIT’s 71% would add roughly 421 attendances a month.

02

Make Studio FIT the template, then scale it

Programming

ReasoningStudio FIT is the studio’s best-performing format by a distance: 71.0% utilisation on 39 sessions, an average class of 7.1, +63 more attendees than last September, and the highest revenue per class of any format at ₹6,999. It achieved this while adding 10 sessions. Only 1% of its attendance is on intro offers — these are committed members.

Expected impactAdding 3 FIT sessions a week at current fill adds about 91 attendances a month, worth roughly ₹89,669 of class revenue, using capacity the studio already owns.

03

Close the early-morning black hole

Studio Manager + Programming

ReasoningSessions starting before 09:00 fill 31.3% — 19 points below the late-morning peak — and account for 55 of the month’s sessions. Eight of the eleven fully empty sessions in September started at 07:30 or 09:15, and every one of them was PowerCycle.

Expected impactConsolidating the weakest early slots into the 09:00–11:00 window, or converting them to a format with proven early demand, would remove about 13 unproductive sessions a month and lift overall utilisation by an estimated 2–3 points.

04

Rebalance the week away from Wednesday

Programming

ReasoningWednesday fills 30.9% against Saturday’s 56.2% — a 25-point gap inside the same week. Wednesday also runs 51 sessions, more than any day except Tuesday, and earns the lowest revenue per class at ₹3,887 against Saturday’s ₹6,152.

Expected impactMoving 4 of Wednesday’s weakest sessions to Saturday and Sunday mornings, where utilisation is 56% and 48%, redirects roughly 122 attendances a month into demand that already exists.

05

Fix the fourth-week fade

Programming + Marketing

ReasoningUtilisation falls from 47.7% in week one to 41.8% in week four while the number of sessions run stays broadly constant. September 2025 showed the identical pattern, which means this is a structural rhythm rather than a September event.

Expected impactHolding week four to the week-one rate would add roughly 40 attendances in a single week. A mid-month re-engagement push aimed at members who have not booked in 14 days is the natural instrument.

06

Stop scheduling classes that draw two people

Programming

Reasoning49 of 259 sessions (19%) ran to two attendees or fewer, including 11 that were completely empty. Those sessions tied up 643 seats on the schedule. PowerCycle accounts for 26 of them.

Expected impactConsolidating the leanest 29 of these sessions would free roughly 385 seat-hours a month and give the studio a timetable it can promote honestly. Every empty class also carries a trainer cost that this data does not capture.

07

Build the conversion pathway that the hosted classes lack

Marketing + Studio Manager

ReasoningAll 3 hosted and partner classes in September ran at 83% utilisation — the fullest classes of the month — and produced ₹0 of class revenue, because every attendee was complimentary. Separately, hosted-class leads convert to membership at 8.3% against 24.2% for referrals.

Expected impactThese are the studio’s best-attended sessions and its worst-converting source. Attaching a booked second class to every hosted attendee at the point of arrival is the cheapest fix available and would move the modelled value of the programme materially without changing what it costs to run.

08

Publish utilisation, not just attendance

Studio Manager

ReasoningThe studio tracks attendance well but the timetable is set on judgement. This September a 25-point utilisation spread existed between two days, a 19-point spread existed between two dayparts, and 6 of 12 formats filled less than 40% of their seats. None of that is visible in an attendance-only report, because attendance is a count and utilisation is a ratio.

Expected impactOne monthly utilisation table, read before the next month’s timetable is built, changes the basis of every scheduling decision from "did anyone come" to "was this the right room".

09

Shrink the room before shrinking the timetable

Studio Manager + Programming

ReasoningRooms of ten to eleven seats ran 62.4% full across 62 sessions; rooms of twelve to thirteen ran 37.3% across 99 sessions, and rooms of fourteen or more ran 38.5% across 98. The studio has already moved in this direction — sessions in ten-to-eleven-seat rooms rose from 49 to 62 — and the effect on the fill rate is arithmetic, not heroics.

Expected impactThe 99 sessions sitting in the twelve-to-thirteen band are the largest single block of addressable inefficiency in the timetable. Capping those rooms at eleven seats removes roughly 198 seat-slots a month that nobody is buying, and lifts overall utilisation by around 6.0 points without changing a single thing about who teaches or when.

10

Put a hard line under complimentary seats

Studio Manager + Finance

ReasoningComplimentary seats rose 57% year on year, to 225 of 1404 attendances — 16.0% of the room, against 9.7% a year earlier. Studio Barre 57 alone ran 27 comp seats on 331 attendances (27%).

Expected impactComps are legitimate but they are invisible in the fill rate and the fill rate is what the timetable is judged on. A monthly comp budget by format — and a rule that a comp consumes the same seat a paying member could have bought — would make the 225 seats visible. At September’s revenue per head of ₹931 that is ₹2,09,475 of delivered value a month to account for.

11

Design the first visit, do not default it

Studio Manager + Programming

ReasoningA first class on a Tuesday leads to a third visit 32.0% of the time; on a Sunday, 14.6%. Before 9am, 27.8%; in the afternoon, 15.9%. In Studio Barre 57, 28.3%; in Studio Mat 57, 11.6%.

Expected impactTrialists are currently placed wherever there is room. Placing them deliberately — into the Tuesday and early-morning slots that convert at nearly double the afternoon rate — costs nothing and operates on the 3025 first-timers this analysis covers. Even a five-point lift in third-visit conversion is worth about ₹5,63,255 of delivered value.

12

Manage the booking book, not the attendance

Studio Manager

ReasoningBookings fell 25% against a 4.9% fall in attendance, and the book now covers only 48.7% of the seats on the board, down from 60.5%. Attendance told the studio after the fact that September was quieter; the booking book said so in advance.

Expected impactA weekly booked-versus-capacity ratio for the coming fortnight, read alongside the fill rate for the past one, converts the timetable from a rear-view report into a leading one. It is the difference between noticing the current quarter and managing the next one.

13

Report frequency per active member, not attendance alone

Studio Manager + Management

ReasoningThe member base is widening while volume falls: 394 members trained this September against 305 last, but each of them came 3.56 times against 4.84. Attendance is a lagging number; visits per active member is the number that moves first.

Expected impactA monthly line for visits per member, sitting beside the member count, would have flagged this decline in the spring instead of at the September review. It costs the studio nothing to produce and it changes what the studio notices.

14

Build a continuity tier from the members who never leave

Studio Manager + CRM

ReasoningOnly 18 members trained at Bandra in all three of September 2024, 2025 and 2026. Against a base of 394 members this September, that is 4.6% who have kept the habit across three years of a business that has run 355 and 305 members in the same months.

Expected impactThese 18 people are the studio’s only proof that a member can stay. They should be known by name, asked what holds them, and used as the benchmark against which every retention initiative is measured. A studio that cannot describe its longest-serving members in detail cannot design for them.

Method and limitations

How to read these numbers, and what they cannot show

Sources and method

Day End Report – Part 3 – Sessions (25,675 rows, exported 11 October 2026) is the primary source. Each row is one class occurrence at one location, with capacity, checked-in, booked, late-cancelled, complimentary, revenue and a breakdown of how attendees paid. Day End Report – Part 3 – Teacher Recurring (3,294 rows) is the same data aggregated per recurring weekly slot and reconciles to the Sessions file exactly.

Utilisation is computed here as checked-in attendances divided by capacity offered, per class occurrence. This is the studio’s own definition and it is the one used throughout. It differs from a count of bookings, and it counts a seat as unused whether the member never booked it or booked and did not turn up.

A note on the recurring-slot file

Two columns in the Teacher Recurring export are mislabelled in the platform: the column named FillRate actually contains revenue per class, and the column named ClassAvgExclEmpty actually contains the fill rate. This report uses only the raw counts from that file — classes, capacity and checked-in — and recomputes every ratio itself.

Known limitations

  • No trainer cost. This data contains no payroll or cost-per-class information, so an empty class can be described as unproductive but not quantified as a loss. Part 1 of the Payroll export supplies teacher economics, and it runs only to August 2026.
  • Revenue attribution. Class revenue is the platform’s allocation of member spend to attended classes. It reconciles to 85% of September cash. It is a sound basis for comparing formats, not an accounting statement.
  • Two sessions of 20:00 and one of 16:00 are too few to draw conclusions from; hour-level figures with fewer than five sessions are marked accordingly in the workbook.
  • September 2025 followed Ganesh Chaturthi (27 August) while September 2026 absorbed it (14 September). Week-by-week comparisons near the festival are affected.

reports.intro: Report four of seven · Membership lifecycle Lapsed and churned memberships Every membership Bandra has ever sold, read forward from the day it was bought. The median paid membership lasts 19 days, 57.0% are finished inside a month, and the way they end is split almost evenly between members who never started and members who quietly stopped. Lapse ledger · 8,707 Bandra membership instances and 3,974 paid memberships Check-in ledger · 3,768 members, 2022 to October 2026 Snapshot 18 October 2026
reports.html:
Start here

The churn book is not a story about losing loyal members. It is a story about memberships that never really began.

Every membership ever sold at Bandra sits in this ledger: 8,707 memberships taken out by 3,768 people, of which 3,974 were paid memberships from 1,699 members. Read forward from purchase, the pattern is stark and consistent across two years of trading: one in five paid memberships ends within a week. More than half end within a month. Only 3.2% are still in force a year later.

The median paid Bandra membership lasts 19 days. Not months — days. And it has shortened: the median membership bought in 2024 ran 29 days, one bought in 2025 ran 17, and one bought so far in 2026 is running 19. Every retention, referral and frequency conversation the studio has depends on that number, and it is getting worse.

The reassuring reading is in how people are lost rather than how many. Among memberships with enough visits to measure a trend, 37.2% ran a second half that was half the first or worse — and 10.5% ended with a second half in which the member did not attend at all. They did not cancel, complain or ask for a refund. They drifted, while the membership was still live and still contactable. That is a recoverable failure, and it is what this report is built around.

The shape of the churn book

93.5% of every membership Bandra has ever sold is now lapsed. The live book is a thin sliver of the lifetime book.

At Bandra the derived statuses read: 7,745 lapsed (89.0%), 371 in a renewal grace period, 352 never activated, 111 active and 77 renewed.

That ratio is less alarming than it looks, because it counts every instance since 2022 including free and promotional entries — 4,519 of the 8,707 rows are complimentary or staff entries rather than purchases. Restricted to paid memberships the picture softens but does not change shape: of 3,974 paid memberships, 89.7% are lapsed and only 8.2% are live or renewing.

What a 43.0% thirty-day survival rate means commercially

A studio that loses 57.0% of its memberships inside a month is not running a retention business. It is running an acquisition business with a very short billing cycle — and every month it must refill 57.0% of the book from scratch simply to stand still. That is the reason the studio’s lead engine has to run as hard as it does, and it reframes acquisition from growth activity into maintenance cost.

The two ways to lose a member

Half the churn is people who never engaged. Half is people who engaged and then withdrew. They need opposite responses.

Sort the paid memberships by how often they cancelled and a useful split appears. 2,084 memberships never cancelled a single class — and they completed an average of just 2.3 sessions. They did not leave because something went wrong; they never arrived. At the other end, 467 memberships cancelled more than half of everything they booked, averaging 10.8 late cancellations each. Those members were present, engaged, and visibly losing the habit before they stopped.

Two failure modes, two fixes. The first is a first-fortnight activation problem — the product was bought and not used. The second is a habit-decay problem — the rhythm broke. A single win-back campaign aimed at both will be efficient at neither, which is why the recommendations in this report keep them apart.

Note how flat the renewal rate is across every band. Cancelling a lot is an early symptom rather than a cause, which is exactly why it is worth acting on the first time it appears.

Did they use what they paid for?

Most did. The ones who did not are identifiable at the point of sale, and they are carrying a lot of unspent money.

Session allowance is recorded for 802 package and credit memberships. Of those, 332 (41.4%) used every class they bought, and a further 103 used more than three-quarters. At the other end, 145 memberships (18.1%) used a quarter or less, leaving 1,953 unused classes in total.

The unused-credit group is the one to act on, commercially as much as humanly. A member who has paid and not attended has received nothing for their money; the studio has banked revenue it will eventually have to earn or give back in goodwill. It is also a countable, visible, unfinished transaction sitting in the CRM: memberships in the lowest usage band are carrying 8 and 7 unspent classes.

The decline that comes first

Almost every lost member slowed down before they stopped. The slowdown is measurable, and it happens while the membership is still live.

Splitting each membership period in half and comparing the two shows the shape of a departure. 10.5% of measurable memberships ended with a second half in which the member did not attend at all, and a further 26.7% more than halved their frequency. Together, 37.2% of memberships ran a second half that was half the first or worse, against just 36.4% that held or grew.

This is a warning the studio already owns and does not use. The decline is visible from the mid-point of any monthly or quarterly cycle. A member whose visits halve in the second fortnight of a one-month membership is stating exactly what is about to happen, and nothing in the current process reads that signal.

Product by product

Commitment length is the only product feature that reliably predicts survival. Price is not.

Sorted by renewal rate the products separate cleanly. The 6-month unlimited renews at 40%, the extended 10-class pack at 22% and the 12-class package at 13%. At the bottom, the 2-for-1 introductory pack renews at 5%, the four-class package at 4% and the ten-class single pack at 1%.

Two things stand out. The 10-class single pack is the worst performer in the range — it sells at almost the same ticket as the 12-class package and converts to a renewal 12 points less often. And the gap between the two is not price; it is whether the member was sold a programme or a quantity.

Who is winnable

The win-back list writes itself, and it is the opposite of the list most studios use.

Sorted by how long it has been since they last came, the paid book splits into three groups with very different economics. 316 members are still warm — in the room within the last sixty days — and they paid an average of ₹23,011 across 14.4 completed classes. A further 378 are cooling, having paid ₹11,862. The remaining 1301 are gone, absent more than six months, and paid only ₹9,525 on average.

The instinct is to chase whoever spent the most over their lifetime. The data says the opposite: the members still worth winning are the ones who have been gone the least time, and they are also the ones who were worth the most. Someone last seen three weeks ago who has paid ₹23,011 is a lapse. Someone last seen two years ago who paid ₹9,525 is a completed relationship.

What the lost book cost

The lapsed memberships represent almost all of the money the studio has taken at Bandra, and most of it was spent fast.

The 3,974 paid Bandra memberships in this ledger represent ₹4,40,74,830 of recorded payments, at an average ticket of ₹11,091. Of that, ₹3,44,72,653 — 78.2% — sits against memberships now recorded as lapsed. That is not money the studio has lost; it is money the studio has already banked against relationships that have ended.

The sharper question is how quickly it was earned. With a median membership lasting 19 days and 57.0% finished inside a month, an average ticket of ₹11,091 is being collected roughly every 19 days and then having to be replaced. The studio is not short of customers. It is short of duration — and duration is the one input that makes every other number in these reports easier.

Recommendations

Nine actions, ordered by the size of the leak they address
01

Run a fourteen-day activation sequence on every membership sold

Studio Manager + CRM

Reasoning42.7% of paid memberships end within fourteen days and 57.0% within thirty, and 2,084 memberships never cancelled a single class because they never booked one. The median paid membership at Bandra lasts 19 days.

Expected impactGetting one in ten of the memberships that currently die inside a fortnight to reach four visits would add roughly 307 members into the active habit band each year. On the studio’s own attendance economics that is the largest single recoverable block in this report.

02

Treat "bought and never attended" as a same-day alert, not a report line

Front Desk + CRM

ReasoningThere are 352 Bandra memberships across 241 people that were paid for and never activated, and the trend is rising: 36 in 2024, 81 in 2025, 235 so far in 2026.

Expected impactA member who has bought and not booked is the highest-intent, lowest-cost call the studio can make. Ringing them within 48 hours of purchase converts a dead transaction into a first visit, and a first visit is the only thing that has ever predicted a second.

03

Put a member on a plan at their first renewal, not a quantity

Studio Manager

ReasoningThe 12-class package renews at 13% while the 10-class single pack renews at 1%, at virtually the same ticket. The 4-class package renews at 4% and the 2-for-1 pack at 5%.

Expected impactThe difference is not price, it is framing. Selling the same money as a scheduled programme rather than a bundle of classes is a script change, not a product change, and it moves the single largest cohort in the book.

04

Write down the unused classes and go and collect them

Studio Manager + CRM

Reasoning1,953 paid classes sit unused across 802 memberships, and 145 memberships used a quarter or less of what they bought. Memberships that used 10% or less of their allowance are carrying 8 unspent classes each.

Expected impactEvery one of those classes has already been paid for. Asking a member to come and use what they own is the least expensive contact the studio can make, it requires no discount and no offer, and it puts a body back in the room.

05

Watch the second half of every membership for the halving signal

CRM

Reasoning37% of memberships show a second half that was half the first or worse, and 10% end with a second half in which the member did not attend at all. Only 36% held or improved.

Expected impactThis is a leading indicator that already exists in the data and is not being read. A member whose visit rate halves in the middle of a membership should trigger a human contact while the membership is still live, not a win-back campaign after it ends.

06

Segment win-back by recency, not by lifetime value

CRM + Marketing

Reasoning316 members were last in the room within 60 days and paid an average of ₹23,011; 1301 have been gone over six months and paid ₹9,525.

Expected impactThe instinct is to chase the biggest historical spenders. The evidence is that recency and value travel together: the recently lapsed are both the most winnable and the most valuable. Re-ranking the win-back list by recency would re-point the same effort at roughly double the average ticket.

07

Separate the two churn mechanisms in every dashboard

CRM + Studio Manager

Reasoning2,084 memberships never booked a class, while 467 cancelled more than half of everything they booked. Both are currently reported as one lapsed number.

Expected impactAn onboarding problem and a habit-decay problem need different owners, different scripts and different timelines. Reporting them as a single churn figure guarantees that the studio treats both with the remedy for whichever is more visible.

08

Freeze, do not lose, the members who are slipping

Front Desk

ReasoningOnly 809 of 3,974 paid memberships ever used a freeze, while 241 members never activated at all and 2,084 never booked.

Expected impactA two-week freeze costs the studio almost nothing, keeps the contract alive, and converts a lapse into a pause. Offering it proactively at the moment attendance drops is cheaper than any win-back campaign and protects the relationship while the member sorts out whatever interrupted it.

09

Price the churn into the acquisition plan

Management

ReasoningAt a 57.0% thirty-day and 76.1% sixty-day end rate, the studio must replace most of its book every two months. That is the real reason the lead engine has to run at 7,822 leads.

Expected impactFraming acquisition as the cost of churn rather than as growth changes what the studio is willing to spend on retention. On this data, a one-point improvement in thirty-day survival removes the need for more acquisition than any campaign the studio could run.

10

Sell the first month as a programme, not a class count

Sales + Front Desk

ReasoningAcross 945 Bandra first-timers with a recorded first purchase, the product they started on predicts almost the whole of their lifetime value. A member whose first purchase was a 1 Month Unlimited is worth ₹74,283 on average; one whose first purchase was a single class is worth ₹13,689. Same studio, same period, same marketing — a 5.4-fold difference decided at the point of sale.

Expected impactThe studio’s entry offer is the cheapest thing it can say yes to, and the cheapest thing is producing the least valuable members. Selling the first month as a timed programme with a named start date, rather than a pack of classes the member can spend at leisure, changes the product without changing the price. The trial class should be an audition for ₹74,283, not a coupon for one session.

11

Book the second visit before the member leaves the building

Front Desk + CRM

ReasoningAmong 1,527 measurable first-timers, lifetime value falls in a straight line with how long the second visit took. Members back within a day are worth ₹39,768 and are retained at 72%. Those whose second visit took a month or never happened are worth ₹13,918 and retained at 95%.

Expected impactThe second visit is worth 2.9 times the third, the tenth or anything after it, because everything after it depends on it. It is also the easiest thing in this report to influence: a member standing at the desk on their first day will say yes to a date. Nobody is currently asking.

12

Read the at-risk band fortnightly, not the lapsed band annually

Studio Manager + CRM

ReasoningOf every Bandra first-timer on file, 3,008 are recorded as churned and 642 as lapsed, against 395 active and only 168 flagged at risk. The members in the at-risk band are worth ₹19,268 each on average against ₹3,812 for the churned band.

Expected impactThe studio has one band where intervention is cheap and one where it is expensive, and the report it reads monthly is weighted towards the second. Moving the same effort one stage earlier — from the members who have already gone to the members whose visits have just slipped — multiplies the yield of every retention hour the team spends.

Sources and method

Lapse ledger: Lapsed New - Lapsed, 29,148 membership instances across all locations, filtered to Supreme HQ, Bandra (8,707 instances, 3,768 members). Paid memberships are those with a recorded amount paid and no staff, complimentary or promotional product name (3,974 instances, 1,699 members). Attendance behaviour is cross-checked against the Day End Part 4 check-in ledger. Membership dates arrive in two formats and are parsed accordingly.
Survival is measured from purchase to the earlier of the churn date and the membership end date; memberships that are still open are treated as surviving to 18 October 2026. Products with fewer than fifteen sales are excluded from product-level rates. Session-allowance and remaining-session fields are populated for package and credit products only.
Figures are gross value as recorded at snapshot, not contribution margin.

reports.title: Supreme HQ, Bandra — Format Comparisons
reports.intro: Report five of seven · Product performance Format comparisons 10 formats, one timetable and one audience. The format that carries 35% of the week fills 35.0% of its seats; the format that carries 15% fills 71.0%. This report compares them on eight measures at once and finds that the studio is not short of demand — it is short of the right demand in the right room. Sessions ledger · 259 classes, September 2026 10 formats compared · 1,404 attendances · ₹13,06,451 attributed revenue Snapshot 18 October 2026
reports.html:
Start here

On revenue, PowerCycle leads. On every measure of efficiency, it is last among the formats that matter.

September 2026 ran 259 classes across 12 formats, drew 1,404 attendances and attributed ₹13,06,451 of revenue to them. But the three largest formats are almost identical in scale and wildly different in behaviour. PowerCycle and Barre 57 together carry 55% of the timetable and fill 35.0% and 44.6% respectively. Studio FIT carries 15% and fills 71.0%.

The reason this is not simply a scheduling problem is visible in the member data. PowerCycle reaches 181 distinct members in the month — more than any other format — while FIT reaches 104. But of FIT’s members, 23.1% came four or more times inside the month. Of PowerCycle’s, 17.1% did. FIT is not a bigger product. It is a stickier one, and the studio is giving the stickier product less than half the week.

The league table

Eight measures, and no format wins all of them. The pattern of who wins what is the finding.

Set the formats side by side and a division of labour emerges that the studio is not currently managing deliberately. FIT wins on fill (71.0%), revenue per class (₹6,999) and regularity (23.1%). Mat 57 is second on fill at 55.1% on a small timetable. PowerCycle leads on absolute attendance simply because it runs 90 sessions. And the express formats — PowerCycle X at 52.6%, Cardio Barre X at 15.3% — are the widest spread in the table, which tells the studio that format length matters more than format family.

Read on revenue per head, however, the differences almost vanish: ₹858 to ₹1,142, a spread of 33%. That is a striking result. It means the audience is worth roughly the same per person wherever they sit. Formats do not differ in the value of the member. They differ in how many members the studio can get into the room.

Reach and regularity are different questions, and the studio currently answers only the first. In September, PowerCycle touched 181 individual members, Barre 57 180 and FIT 104. But a member who comes once counts the same as a member who comes daily. Measured by the share of a format’s audience that attended at least four times in the month, the order reverses: FIT 23.1%, PowerCycle 17.1%, Barre 57 10.0%, and the smaller formats fall to 4.8% and below.

The average member of each format tells the same story. A FIT attendee came 2.66 times in the month; a Barre 57 attendee 1.84; a Mat 57 attendee 1.55. Meanwhile 64% of Mat 57’s attendees and 61% of Cardio Barre’s came exactly once in the month.

Complimentary attendance is concentrated, and it lands on the formats with the most loyal paying audiences.

Across the studio 225 attendances were complimentary in September. They are not evenly spread. Recommendations

Nine actions, ordered by the size of the opportunity each addresses
01

Rebuild PowerCycle around the room it actually fills

ReasoningPowerCycle carries 35% of the timetable and fills 35.0% of its seats, against Studio FIT at 71.0% on 15% of the timetable. Its express variant fills 52.6% in roughly half the room.

Expected impactCutting the average PowerCycle class to eleven seats removes about 180 seat-slots a month that nobody is buying, and lifts the studio-wide utilisation rate on its own.

02

Scale Studio FIT deliberately

Programming

ReasoningFIT is the best-performer on every efficiency measure: 71.0% fill, ₹6,999 revenue per class, and 23.1% of its attendees came four or more times inside the month — the highest regularity of any format.

Expected impactAdding three FIT sessions a week at the current average of 7.1 attendees, at ₹985 a head, is worth about ₹90,283 of class revenue a month from capacity the studio already owns.

03

Treat the express formats as a distinct product, not a short version

Programming + Marketing

ReasoningPowerCycle Express fills 52.6% against its parent at 35.0%, and Cardio Barre fills 27.6% against Cardio Barre Express at 15.3%. The express formats are not simply weaker — at their best they beat the full-length class in a smaller room.

Expected impactExpress formats cost less to deliver, fill a harder slot and suit a member who cannot commit ninety minutes. Building two or three deliberate express slots into peak commuter windows is a cheaper capacity expansion than adding full-length classes.

04

Market the multi-format ladder as the product

Marketing + Studio Manager

ReasoningMembers who have used one format have paid an average of ₹3,307 and completed 1.7 classes. Those who have used three formats have paid ₹15,687 and completed 8.3. At five formats the figure is ₹18,497 on 13.9 classes.

Expected impactOnly 38.7% of members have used three or more formats. Moving one member in ten up one rung of the ladder is the single largest value lever in this report, and it needs a product and a script rather than a discount.

05

Fix the formats nobody is asked to try

Programming + Front Desk

ReasoningStudio Mat 57 reaches 83 members at 55.1% fill with only 4.8% returning four or more times. Cardio Barre reaches 51 at 27.6% with 2.0% regulars.

Expected impactThese are good products with almost no habit attached. A single well-chosen pairing — Mat 57 as the recovery companion to Barre 57, Cardio Barre as the first step toward Barre 57 — turns two under-used rooms into a route rather than a stop.

06

Set the comp budget by format, not in total

Studio Manager + Finance

ReasoningComplimentary seats run at 27.2% of Barre 57 attendance against 4.0% for FIT. Across the studio that is 225 free seats, worth ₹2,09,367 at the studio’s own revenue per head.

Expected impactA per-format comp allowance makes an invisible number visible. It also stops the formats with the most loyal paying audiences from quietly absorbing the markdowns that belong to the studio as a whole.

07

Use the day grid to re-time, not to cut

Programming

ReasoningEvery major format has at least one day it owns: Back Body Blaze peaks on Wed, Barre 57 peaks on Sat, Cardio Barre peaks on Wed, Cardio Barre X peaks on Fri. The same formats are weak on their worst day by a wide margin.

Expected impactThe cheapest utilisation gain available is to move sessions from a format’s weakest day to its strongest, and from a format that is weak at that hour to one that is strong. That is a scheduling exercise, not a product decision, and it costs nothing to trial for a month.

08

Report formats by their member economics, not their revenue

Management

ReasoningRanked by revenue the formats read PowerCycle, Barre 57, FIT. Ranked by fill they read FIT, Mat 57, PowerCycle X. Ranked by members reached they read PowerCycle 181, Barre 57 180, FIT 104. Ranked by how many of those members become regulars they read FIT first by a distance.

Expected impactA single monthly page carrying utilisation, members reached, regularity and revenue per head gives the studio four views of the same product. The current revenue-only view systematically favours the format with the most sessions.

09

Watch the formats whose devotees drift

CRM + Programming

ReasoningMembers whose favourite format is PowerCycle have been absent an average of 373 days; for FIT devotees it is 245 days. The value of a FIT devotee is ₹22,621 against ₹10,428 for PowerCycle, on 21.2 against 8.7 classes.

Expected impactFavourite format is a useful early-warning field the studio already collects and does not read. A monthly count of members whose favourite format has gone quiet is a churn watch-list that costs nothing to produce.

10

Judge a format on twelve sessions or not at all

Programming

Reasoning7 of the 12 formats Bandra ran in September appeared fewer than twelve times — between them 36 sessions out of 259. The express formats ran 12 sessions in the month between them, filling 15% to 53%.

Expected impactA format that runs six times a month cannot be judged on fill rate, and it cannot be judged on revenue either. Either give a new format a real commitment — a fixed weekly slot for a full quarter — or stop reporting on it. The studio is currently making programming decisions about formats it has barely tested.

11

Let the length of a class decide, not the family it belongs to

Programming + Studio Manager

ReasoningInside the same format family the results separate sharply. PowerCycle Express fills 53% across 6 sessions; Cardio Barre Express fills 15% across 6. One is a premium express product, the other is an afternoon of empty seats.

Expected impactThe studio’s own timetable already contains the answer to its utilisation problem, in miniature: a short, specific, well-named class sells, and an unspecified short version of a long class does not. Every express format should be rebuilt to the PowerCycle Express template — its own name, its own benefit, its own slot — before any of them is withdrawn.

12

Put revenue per class next to fill rate in every programming review

Studio Manager + Finance

ReasoningAcross September the correlation between a format’s fill rate and its revenue per class is almost total — FIT fills 71% and earns ₹6,999 a class; PowerCycle fills 35% and earns ₹4,363. The two columns rank the formats the same way.

Expected impactFill rate flatters formats with small rooms and penalises formats that were given the big ones, so any review that reads fill alone will keep making the same mistake. Revenue per class is the number that survives the comparison, and pairing it with the studio’s cost per session turns a programming debate into an arithmetic one.

Sources and method

Capacity is per session (total capacity divided by the number of classes recorded on the row). Member reach and regularity from the Day End Part 4 check-in ledger, attended entries only. Favourite-format and format-count fields from the lapse ledger, which records the formats against each membership.
Formats with one or fewer sessions in the month are excluded from the comparison tables. Revenue is class-attributed revenue as recorded, not contribution margin, and a complimentary seat earns nothing by construction.

reports.title: Supreme HQ, Bandra — Late Cancellations and Discounts
reports.intro: Report six of seven · Booking behaviour and price Late cancellations and discounts Two ways a studio gives away value: a seat booked and released too late, and a price quietly marked down. In September, Bandra released 199 seats late. In 2026 it has given away ₹25,57,453 in discounts at a depth of 13.2% — the deepest it has ever discounted. This report measures both, and separates the part of each that is a real problem from the part that is simply the cost of running a studio. Cancellation ledger · 10,656 late cancellations, 2024 to October 2026 Sales ledger · 6,547 line items · ₹55,02,355 of discount on file Snapshot 18 October 2026
reports.html:
Start here

Booking discipline has genuinely improved. Discounting has genuinely worsened. Both are choices, and only one is being managed.

Start with the good news, because it is real and it is measurable. Across every seat booked at Bandra this year, 86.3% were attended and only 12.9% became a late cancellation. In 2025 those figures were 72.8% and 27.1%; in 2024, 80.4% and 19.2%. Late cancellations fell from 6,660 seats in 2025 to 2,064 this year, while the number of attending visits rose. Whatever changed in how the studio communicates expections around bookings, it worked.

In September 2026 specifically, 199 seats were released late against 1,404 attendances. That is 14.2 late cancellations for every hundred classes attended — a level the studio can live with, and one it can reduce further.

The discount story moves the other way. The studio discounted ₹25,57,453 in 2026 so far, at a depth of 13.2% of gross, against 8.0% in 2024. Discount spread has fallen — fewer sales carry an offer — but the offers that are made are deeper, and they are concentrated on the products that needed them least. That is the finding worth acting on.

What a released seat costs

A late cancellation is a seat the studio paid for and did not use. Whether that matters depends entirely on how full the room was.

The value of a released seat is not fixed. It is worth almost nothing in a half-empty room and a great deal in a full one. In September the board ran at 48.7% occupancy on the booking book when those 199 seats were released, against 60.5% in September 2025. More than half the seats were unsold at the moment they were given back.

That changes the remedy. Charging for a late cancellation recovers a little; reselling the seat recovers the whole ticket and keeps the member. And the seats are not evenly distributed: 64 of them were PowerCycle, 52 FIT and 39 Barre 57, so the recovery problem is concentrated in the three formats that between them carry most of the week.

Who cancels, and when

Cancelling is concentrated, and it is concentrated among the studio’s most engaged members.

In September 110 members released a booked seat late. But 68 of them did it once and 29 did it three times or more, and the ten heaviest accounts for 23.6% of every cancellation in the month. Across the entire paid membership book the concentration is starker still: the worst tenth of memberships account for 80.3% of all 10,104 late cancellations ever recorded.

The timing says something the studio can use. Cancellations cluster at 9:00, 11:00, 18:00, the mid-morning block, and again in the early evening — the two windows where the studio’s paying demand is strongest. By day, Thursday and Saturday carry the most. These are not random acts of forgetfulness; they are the hours where a working member’s day most often gets in the way.

What cancelling actually predicts

It does not predict leaving. It predicts a member whose week has stopped fitting — which is more useful.

Sort the 3,974 paid memberships by how often they cancelled and a clear picture emerges. Members who never cancelled completed an average of 2.3 classes. Those who cancelled more than half of everything they booked completed 10.0 and averaged 10.8 late cancellations each. Between those two extremes, engagement rises before it falls: the members who cancel a little attend more than the members who never cancel at all.

And yet the renewal rate barely moves across the bands — 6.6% to 13.3%. Cancelling is a symptom, not a cause. That is precisely why it is valuable: it appears weeks before the member stops coming, it is already recorded, and nobody reads it.

The studio is giving away more per sale than ever, to fewer sales, and mostly on the products that did not need it.

At the same time the spread narrowed — 24% of sales carried a discount in 2024 against 18% this year. The studio has stopped discounting casually and started discounting decisively, which is a different behaviour, not obviously a better one.

The codes read as a calendar of the studio’s campaigns: anniversary offers, a new-customer code, festival and self-love promotions. Two codes alone account for the largest single blocks of value given away this year.

Do discounts work?

Pooled, they look like the best investment the studio makes. Controlled for what was bought, the effect disappears — and in places reverses.

Take every first-time buyer whose first purchase is at least six months old and split them by whether that first purchase carried a discount. Pooled, the answer is spectacular: discounted first-buyers repeat at 67.4% and are worth ₹62,483 in lifetime value, against 44.5% and ₹17,841 for those who paid full price.

That comparison is not fair, because the products that carry discounts are not the products that carry full price. Hold the product constant and the picture changes:

12 Class Package — discounted first-buyers repeat at 77.3% against 94.0% for full-price buyers, with lifetime value of ₹54,975 against ₹1,02,470.
1 Month Unlimited — discounted first-buyers repeat at 83.7% against 91.2% for full-price buyers, with lifetime value of ₹80,308 against ₹1,07,053.

The pooled advantage was composition. Members who happened to start on an unlimited or package product were always going to stay longer, and those products happen to carry the offers. On this evidence the studio has no proof that its discounts buy loyalty — only that they reduce the price of sales it would largely have made anyway. That is a testable proposition, and it is not currently being tested.
