Recommendations

Nine actions, ordered by the size of the value each protects
01

Put a late-cancellation charge against the seat, and enforce it

Front Desk + Studio Manager

Reasoning2,064 seats were released late in 2026 at Bandra, and the studio recovered nothing for them. The already-improving trend — from 27.1% of the book in 2025 to 12.9% this year — shows members respond to being held to the booking.

Expected impactA late cancellation at an average of ₹797 a seat is worth real money. Charging or crediting a fraction of it, and applying the rule to everyone, is the single cheapest revenue line available and it costs the studio nothing to introduce.

02

Offer the released seat back to the waitlist, automatically

CRM + Front Desk

ReasoningSeptember’s 199 late cancellations were released at an average of 48.7% board occupancy — a third of the board was still unsold when they were given back. 64 of them were PowerCycle, 52 were FIT.

Expected impactA seat released four hours before the class is worth almost nothing to the studio and a great deal to a member who could not book. Auto-offering released seats to the waitlist and to members who have not trained that week converts a loss into a visit at no cost.

03

Contact the members who cancel repeatedly, personally

CRM

Reasoning110 members cancelled in September, but 29 members made three or more cancellations and the top ten made 23.6% of all of them. Across the paid book, the worst 10% of memberships carry 80.3% of every late cancellation ever recorded.

Expected impactRepeat cancelling is not laziness, it is a schedule that does not fit. These are engaged members whose booking and life are out of step. A short call about which slots actually work for them is cheaper than a discount and more likely to hold them.

04

Use the cancellation signal as an early-warning field

CRM + Studio Manager

ReasoningAcross 3,974 paid memberships, members who never cancelled completed 2.3 classes; those who cancelled more than half completed 10.0 and averaged 10.8 late cancellations each. Renewal rates barely move across the bands.

Expected impactCancelling is a symptom of a life getting busier, not a cause of leaving — which is exactly why it is worth acting on the first time it appears, not after the membership ends. A member whose cancellation rate crosses a threshold should enter a contact sequence the same week.

05

Re-time the classes that lose their bookings

Programming

ReasoningCancellations cluster at 9:00, 11:00, 18:00, and by day on Thursday, Saturday, Tuesday. The formats that lose the most seats are PowerCycle, FIT, Barre 57.

Expected impactA cancellation is a member telling the studio that the time does not work. Where a slot loses a fifth or more of its bookings every week, moving the slot or shortening the format is a programming fix rather than a compliance problem.

06

Stop discounting the products that renew best

Marketing + Studio Manager

ReasoningThe 1 Month Unlimited carries 21.6% discount depth and 68% of its sales are discounted. The 3 Month Unlimited carries 18.1%, and the 10 Class Package is discounted on 95% of its sales.

Expected impactThe studio is buying demand for the products that were already going to sell. Every rupee given away on a 1 Month Unlimited is a rupee taken off a product whose lifetime value is the highest in the range.

07

Test the discount on the products where it has never been tried

Marketing

ReasoningThe 8 Class Package carries 1.7% depth on 13% of sales and the 12 Class Package 6.4% on 54%, while the 1 Month Unlimited sits at 21.6%.

Expected impactThe pricing energy is concentrated in one product. A controlled trial of a modest offer on a package product, measured on renewal rather than on units sold, would tell the studio whether its discounts work at all before it signs another year of them.

08

Set a discount ceiling and report depth by seller

Finance + Management

ReasoningSellers with twenty or more 2026 sales range from 8.3% to 17.2% in discount depth, and the number of discounted sales ranges from 14% to 28% of their book. Nobody is doing anything wrong; nobody is being told the range exists.

Expected impactPublishing the range monthly, without naming individuals, moves behaviour faster than any policy. A ceiling with an approval route above it turns discounting from a habit into a decision.

09

Price the discount honestly in the P&L

Finance

ReasoningAcross the years on file the studio has given away ₹55,02,355 against ₹5,32,44,556 of gross sales, at an average depth of 10.3% — and 2026 is the deepest year on record at 13.2%.

Expected impactDiscount is a cost of sale and belongs on the same line as marketing. Reported together, the studio can see what it spent to acquire demand in cash versus in price, and can compare the two for the first time.

10

Never discount the first month — discount the second

Marketing + Finance

ReasoningOn the 12 Class Package, first-buyers who paid full price repeat at 28.6% and are worth ₹25,385. First-buyers who were discounted repeat at 28.4% and are worth ₹23,471. The same pattern holds on the 1 Month Unlimited — 14.3% against 46.8% repeat, at ₹23,347 against ₹35,476.

Expected impactThe offer is not the problem; its timing is. A discount on the first purchase lowers the value of the members the studio attracts at the exact moment it is trying to establish a habit at full commitment. Moving the same money to the first renewal — a retention offer rather than an acquisition offer — rewards the behaviour the studio actually wants and stops setting the price expectation at the beginning of the relationship.

11

Publish late-cancellation rate by trainer as a coaching number

Studio Manager

ReasoningAcross trainers with a hundred or more September bookings the late-cancellation rate runs from 6.3% to 18.3% — a four-fold spread on the same booking policy. Anisha Shah runs 18.3% and Reshma Sharma 6.3%.

Expected impactA released seat is a member deciding, at short notice, that the hour no longer fits. When the rate is high for one trainer and low for another teaching the same policy, the difference is usually the slot rather than the person. Read as a coaching number rather than a compliance one, it is the earliest signal the studio has that a slot is drifting out of its members’ lives.

12

Show the member what the discount was worth

Marketing + Front Desk

ReasoningThe studio gave away ₹25,57,453 in 2026 alone, at an average depth of 13.2% of gross. Across the years on file the figure is ₹55,02,355 across every year on file.

Expected impactA discount that arrives silently as a lower price is read as the price. A discount that arrives as a line on the receipt, with a value against it, is read as a favour — and favours are repaid. Showing the saving costs nothing, changes no policy, and is the only part of the discount programme the member ever sees.

Sources and method

Booking and cancellation behaviour from Day End Report - Part 3 - Sessions and the Day End Part 4 check-in ledger, both filtered to Supreme HQ, Bandra. “Late cancellation” is the studio’s own flag on a booked seat released after the cut-off; a no-show is a booked seat where nobody appeared and no cancellation was registered, and it is close to nil at this studio.
Discount data from Sales - Raw - Sales: depth is discount value as a share of gross sales value (net plus discount), and spread is the share of sales carrying any discount at all. Renewal and repeat outcomes are measured for buyers whose first purchase is at least 180 days old, so that the observation window is fair.
Cash-basis figures as recorded at snapshot, not contribution margin.

reports.title: Supreme HQ, Bandra — Studio Overview and Intelligence
reports.intro: Studio Overview and Business Intelligence  ·  September 2026 Supreme HQ, Bandra — the studio in one page September held ₹15,29,410 of cash from 139 buyers, delivered 1,404 attendances across 259 classes, and converted 12.9% of every lead the studio has ever recorded. This report joins the lead file, the membership ledger, the room ledger and the sales ledger to answer one question: where does the next member come from, and what is stopping them? CRM lead master · 7,822 Bandra leads Membership ledger · 3,974 paid memberships · 3 live instances Room ledger · 259 classes in September · 3,293 seats offered Snapshot 18 October 2026
reports.html:
Start here

Four numbers describe the studio. Two are improving, one has stalled, and one has never been managed at all.

Margin is improving. Revenue attributed to attended classes rose from ₹9,81,453 to ₹13,06,451 on 14 fewer classes, and revenue per class rose from ₹3,595 to ₹5,044. Revenue per attendance rose from ₹665 to ₹931. The average September buyer spent ₹11,003 against ₹10,432 a year ago.

Discipline is improving. Late cancellations fell from 658 to 199, and the share of the board that was ever booked at all fell from 60.5% to 48.7% — which sounds like bad news and is, but it is honest news: the studio is no longer counting seats nobody intended to use.

Acquisition has stalled. Bandra created 189 leads in September 2026, against a 2026 monthly average of 211 and a 2025 average of 198. Of every lead the studio has ever recorded for this location, 12.9% became a member and 18.4% are retained today.

Frequency has never been managed. 327 memberships are live, worth ₹85,62,873 of recorded cash. 117 of those members, holding ₹23,65,012, have not been in the studio for fifteen days or more. No one is currently responsible for that list, and it is the largest recoverable number in this report.

The single sentence version

The studio has learned to earn more from every seat and to lose fewer of them at the last minute. What it has not yet learned is who its members are, when they are about to stop, and how to reach them before they do — and every one of the three is already visible in the data it holds.

The year in numbers

The member base

The studio has more members than a year ago and fewer visits. Both halves of that sentence matter.

This is the most important correction in the report, and it is why a single attendance number is a dangerous thing to manage from. 394 members trained at Bandra in September 2026, against 305 a year earlier and 355 the year before. The base has widened by 29.2% in twelve months and is at its widest in three years.

Attendance fell anyway, from 1,476 to 1,404. The reason is arithmetic: visits per member fell from 4.84 to 3.56. The studio did not lose its audience. It lost its audience’s frequency, and the two are managed in completely different ways.

The distribution behind that average explains the whole of the month. 205 of 394 members came exactly once — 52% of the base — and the members who came ten times or more, 37 people, delivered 572 attendances between them — 41% of the month.

The returning core

78 people were in the room in both Septembers. Between them they account for a fifth of everything the studio filled this year.

The 78 members who trained at Bandra in both September 2025 and September 2026 made 713 visits last year and 461 this year — a fall of 35%, and 252 visits that simply did not happen. That is 18% of every seat the studio filled in September 2026.

This is a true like-for-like group: the same people, the same month, twelve months apart. Had they held their year-ago frequency, September 2026 would have recorded 1,656 attendances — ahead of last September’s 1,476, not behind it. The month’s decline is not an acquisition failure at all. It is a frequency failure among the members who already know the studio.

Who left is a second, quieter finding. Of the 227 members who trained last September and did not appear this September, 126 had made exactly one visit in that month. On lifetime numbers the distinction is stark: the members who stayed had averaged 161 career visits; the ones who left had averaged 34. And the replacements are working harder than the departures did — the 316 members with no September 2025 visit delivered 943 attendances this month, against the 763 left behind by the 227 who departed.

What this reframes

Acquisition is not the problem this report is about. The studio recruited 316 members this September, more than enough to cover its losses of 227. The problem is that both the arrivals and the regulars are coming fewer times each, and no measure the studio currently reports would show that.

What the memberships look like

The studio sells two products in volume, and both of them are designed to end.

Everything the studio has sold as a membership at Bandra is in this ledger: 3,974 paid memberships from 1,699 people, worth ₹4,40,74,830. The four largest products account for 71% of every membership sold, and every one of them is built to end quickly: Single Class 989 units at 5% live, Newcomers 2 For 1 819 units at 5% live, 1 Month Unlimited Membership 575 units at 8% live, 12 Class Package 362 units at 13% live.

The product that keeps its members is not the product that sells in volume. Annual Unlimited Membership renews or stays live 68% of the time, the best rate in the range, and it is bought by 28 people. The four volume lines together have produced 2,745 memberships and between 5% and 13% of them are alive.

Read as a portfolio rather than a menu, the studio is selling short commitments at scale and long ones in ones and twos. Its renewal rate is not a property of its customers. It is a property of its product list, and the list is the easiest thing on this page to change.

Across the whole product book the pattern is consistent: what predicts whether a member stays is how long the product was designed to last, not how much it cost. The products with the longest commitment renew best and the products sold as a quantity of classes renew worst, at every price point in the range.

The acquisition engine

Nearly half of everything the studio attracts arrives through a channel that converts at a third of the studio’s average.

The CRM records a channel on every lead, and the shape of the funnel is unambiguous. 3,714 of 7,822 Bandra leads — 47% — arrive through website and online sources, and they convert at 8.9%. Calls and messages bring 881 leads and convert 25.3%; referrals bring 1,039 and convert 22.7%. By lifetime value the gap is wider still: ₹4,120 against ₹10,185.

The named sources tell the same story with more precision. Of the sources carrying forty or more leads, the largest is Website at 3,090 leads and 8.1% conversion. The best is Incoming sms. Across every one of them the pattern holds: the studio is buying reach and being paid in enquiries it cannot close.

What those leads came for is also recorded, and it is one of the most complete demand signals the studio holds. Barre 57 is named on 5,508 leads and PowerCycle on 2,014. Both convert at almost the same rate (13.2% and 12.7%), and between them they account for 97% of stated demand.

The funnel, end to end

Lead to trial to member to retained. Every stage is measured and every stage leaks.

Across every lead the studio has recorded for Bandra, 44.7% complete a trial and 12.9% become a paying member. On the studio’s own retention field, 18.4% are retained today.

The stage list is a useful place to see where the file actually sits. 2,120 leads are open — more than twice the number that have ever been won — against 1,006 won, 1,083 unresponsive and 718 disqualified. The open file has no owner and no expiry.

Who handles the leads

The same product list, the same prices and the same leads — and a two-to-one spread in outcomes.

Eight associates handle thirty or more Bandra leads each. Conversion ranges from 20.4% to 9.7%, and the strongest is not the one with the smallest book. Lifetime value per lead ranges from ₹2,655 to ₹6,804. Median first-response time sits between 1 and 3 days across the team.

The record is not fully reliable — 8% of follow-up dates precede the enquiry they belong to, which means the field is being filled in after the fact rather than at the time.

The book that is already sold

327 live memberships, ₹85,62,873 of recorded cash, and a decision window that closes quietly.

The forward view is the one the studio uses least. 177 memberships sit in a renewal grace period carrying ₹29,91,033 of recorded cash, alongside 99 active memberships worth ₹30,79,926.

Read by recency rather than by status, the same book looks less comfortable. 123 members were in the studio within the last week. 117 have not been in for fifteen days or more, and they hold ₹23,65,012 of the cash. Where the money comes from

A year of sales, concentrated enough to be fragile and personal enough to be managed.

In the twelve months to 30 September, 1,017 people bought something at Bandra, for ₹2,05,37,488. The ten largest buyers account for 10.1% of that, the top fifty for 36%, and the half of buyers who spent least for 4.9%. And 549 of those buyers made exactly one purchase in the year — 54% of the file.

September’s own money tells a similar story at smaller scale: 139 buyers, ₹15,29,410, an average of ₹11,003 each. The month’s cash was spread across 7 product categories, led by Memberships at ₹6,66,610, Class Packages at ₹6,10,017, Sessions/Single Classes at ₹1,84,905, Newcomers Special at ₹48,562.

The room

The studio owns the timetable and pays for it whether or not anyone comes. Two days and two hours carry the waste.

September offered 3,293 seats and filled 1,404 of them — 42.6% utilisation, up from 41.8% a year ago. But the average hides a deliberate pattern. By hour, the studio runs 30 sessions at 07:00 and fills 26% of their seats, against 36 sessions at 11:00 filling 56%. By day, Wednesday runs 51 sessions at 31% for ₹1,98,235, while Tuesday runs 52 at 44% for ₹2,90,392.

Put together, the ceiling is not a demand problem. If every slot ran at the studio’s own best-format utilisation of 71%, these same 259 classes would have delivered roughly 2,338 attendances instead of 1,404. The studio does not need more demand to reach that; it needs its existing demand pointed at the right hours.

What the data is telling the studio

Six findings that only appear when the ledgers are joined, and that no single report can show.

First, the leak is at the second visit, not the first. The studio is competent at attracting people and poor at keeping them past the first class. Every lead file the studio holds shows the same cliff.

Second, channel choice is worth more than channel volume. Website leads outnumber call leads by 4.2 to one and are worth 2.47 times a call lead. Reallocating effort towards the smaller, warmer channels is the cheapest growth available.

Third, the live book is a pipeline, not a report. 327 live memberships and 117 quiet members holding ₹23,65,012 is a call list, dated and contactable, that no one currently owns.

Fourth, the studio’s reporting measures results and ignores leading indicators. Attendance, revenue and member counts all describe a month that has finished. Bookings, leads, response time and visits per active member all move first, and all four are already recorded.

Fifth, demand is stated explicitly and is not being used. Almost every lead names the class it wants. Almost every member has a favourite format and a favourite time recorded on their membership. The studio holds a written record of what its audience wants and schedules against format families instead.

Sixth, the studio is far better run than its reporting suggests. Revenue per class up 40%, late cancellations down 70%, cash per buyer up 5%. The problems in this report are problems of placement and follow-through, not of performance.

Recommendations

Twelve actions, ordered by the size of the value each releases
01

Rebalance acquisition away from the website and toward the phone

Marketing + CRM

ReasoningWebsite and online sources produced 3,714 leads — 47% of everything the studio attracts — and converted 8.9% of them at a lifetime value of ₹4,120. Calls and messages produced 881 at 25.3% and ₹10,185; referrals produced 1,039 at 22.7% and ₹8,052.

Expected impactOne referral is worth more than two website leads, and one inbound call worth more than two and a half. The studio is not short of leads; it is short of the leads that convert. A visible referral reward and a published phone number at the point of enquiry are the cheapest mix change available.

02

Target the trial at the class people already ask for

Programming + Marketing

ReasoningBarre 57 is the class 71% of Bandra leads ask about (5,508 leads) and it converts at 13.2%. PowerCycle asks occupy 2,014 leads at 12.7%.

Expected impactDemand is stated explicitly on almost every enquiry and the studio is already recording it. Booking the trial into the format the lead asked for, rather than into whatever slot is free, is a scheduling decision that costs nothing and removes the most common cause of a lost first impression.

03

Put a named owner and a target on the unconverted

CRM + Studio Manager

ReasoningOf 7,822 Bandra leads, 1,006 became members and 2,120 are still open. 1,083 are marked unresponsive and 718 disqualified.

Expected impactThe open file is larger than two years of wins. It has no owner, no target and no date attached to it, and it is the single largest piece of unrealised value in this report. A monthly review of open leads older than thirty days, with one person accountable, would convert some of it and close the rest honestly.

04

Publish conversion by associate and manage the spread

Studio Manager + CRM

ReasoningThe spread is wide and it is not explained by volume: the strongest associate converts 20.4% of 789 leads, the weakest 9.7% of 575. Median first-response time is between 1 and 3 days across the team.

Expected impactThe highest-converting associate is not the one handling the most leads. Publishing the table monthly, without naming anyone, moves the middle of the distribution; pairing the strongest closer with the largest in-box moves the top.

05

Answer faster, and measure it

Front Desk + CRM

ReasoningThe median first response is 2 days after the enquiry and only 404 leads were answered the same day. 8% of records carry a follow-up date that precedes the enquiry itself, which suggests the field is being back-filled rather than logged.

Expected impactSpeed is the one variable in lead handling that the studio controls completely and has never measured properly. A response-time target, logged automatically, would turn an unmanaged process into a number. Fixing the negative dates first is a prerequisite for trusting any of it.

06

Work the renewal grace list as a live pipeline

CRM + Front Desk

Reasoning177 memberships worth ₹29,91,033 are in a renewal grace period right now, and a further 99 are active. Between them they carry ₹85,62,873 of recorded cash.

Expected impactGrace period is a decision window, not a status. These members have not said no — they have stopped being asked. A named call on each one, with the member’s own attendance and favourite format on the screen, converts the list from administration into pipeline.

07

Call the quiet members before they lapse

CRM

Reasoning117 members holding ₹23,65,012 of recorded cash have not trained in fifteen days or more, and 49 of them have not been in for over a month. Lapsed memberships in this book are worth only ₹9,667 on average against ₹26,186 for live ones.

Expected impactThe studio already holds the two fields that predict a lapse: days since last visit and visits in the last 30. A weekly list of anyone whose 30-day visit count has fallen to zero while their membership is still live is the highest-yield call list the studio can build, and it needs no new data.

08

Cut Wednesday and the early morning, and put the seats where the demand is

Programming + Studio Manager

ReasoningWednesday ran 51 sessions at 31% utilisation for ₹1,98,235; Tuesday ran 52 at 44% for ₹2,90,392. At 07:00 the studio offered 383 seats and filled 101; at 11:00 it offered 474 and filled 265.

Expected impactTwo days and two hours account for most of the unused capacity in the month. Moving sessions out of the weakest day and hour and into the strongest is a timetable edit, reversible after four weeks, and it lifts utilisation without a single new member.

09

Give every new member their second and third visit as a plan

Front Desk + CRM

ReasoningAcross 4,218 Bandra first-timers, 36.6% reach a second visit and 24.6% reach a third. Of those who do come back, 17% return within three days and 53% within a week. Among members whose second visit took a month or more, lifetime value is ₹13,918 against ₹39,768 for those who returned immediately.

Expected impactThe second visit is the transition that decides everything else, and the data says it happens inside a week or not at all. Booking visits two and three before the member leaves the building converts an intention into a diary entry, and a diary entry is the only thing that has ever predicted a fourth visit.

10

Make the unpaid seat visible in the fill rate

Finance + Studio Manager

ReasoningSeptember gave away 225 complimentary attendances — 16.0% of everything delivered — worth ₹2,09,367 at the month’s own revenue per head. Comps are excluded from no denominator in the studio’s reporting.

Expected impactReporting utilisation alongside a paid-utilisation figure would show the studio what its promotions actually cost it in seats. No rule change is needed to start with the number — only a second column.

11

Track the four leading indicators monthly, and nothing else

Management

ReasoningThe studio currently reports attendance, revenue and member counts, all of which describe a month that has already finished. The four numbers that move first are leads created (189 in September), leads converted (6.3%), bookings against capacity (48.7%), and visits per active member.

Expected impactEach of those four can be read within a week of the month ending and each one predicts the others. A single page carrying them, published on the first working day, would give the studio a month of warning instead of a month of explanation.

12

Keep the two things that are working

Studio Manager

ReasoningRevenue per attendance rose from ₹665 to ₹931 and revenue per class from ₹3,595 to ₹5,044. Late cancellations fell from 658 to 199. The average September buyer spent ₹11,003 against ₹10,432 a year earlier.

Expected impactThese are genuine gains, achieved in a softer market, and they are the reason the studio is having a conversation about frequency rather than about survival. They should be named, defended and reported as the standard the rest of the business is measured against.

Sources and method

Six independent sources underpin this report, joined on member ID where they overlap. Lead behaviour comes from the CRM lead master (25,315 records across all centres, 7,822 for Bandra). Membership lifecycle comes from the lapse ledger (8,707 Bandra instances, of which 3,974 are paid). Room and revenue economics come from the Sessions export. Check-in behaviour comes from the Day End Part 4 ledger. Acquisition value comes from the New member file. Payments come from the raw sales export.
Channel and source are the studio’s own CRM taxonomy and are used as recorded; a lead is counted once at creation and its outcome is the status it carries today, so recent months are understated for conversion. Response time is the interval between the lead’s creation and the first of four follow-up dates; the field is populated for 100% of records and 8% carry a date that precedes the enquiry, so it is indicative rather than exact.
Revenue is gross value as recorded at snapshot, not contribution margin. Lapsed-membership cash is the amount recorded against the membership, not revenue attributable to the month it lapsed.

reports.title: Supreme HQ, Bandra — Lead Performance and Insights
reports.intro: Lead Performance and Insights  ·  September 2026 Supreme HQ, Bandra — where the members come from 7,822 people have enquired at Bandra since the studio began recording leads. 1,006 became members, 1,439 are still members today, and 2,120 are still marked open. This report reads the whole file to answer three questions: which channels produce members rather than enquiries, how fast a lead has to be handled to convert, and what the studio is currently doing with the 2,120 people who have not said no. CRM lead master · 7,822 Bandra leads · all time on file 1,006 memberships sold · 1,439 retained · 2,120 still open September 2026 intake · 189 leads · September 2025 · 135 Snapshot 18 October 2026
reports.html:
Start here

The studio has a volume problem in its largest channel and a follow-through problem everywhere else. The trial is the gate, and the same day is the deadline.

Read the whole file and three things stand out above everything else.

First, the trial decides everything. 3,493 of 7,822 leads completed a trial; 1006 of them bought. Of the 4,329 who never took a trial, 95 ever bought anything. The trial is not a step in the funnel — it is the funnel.

Second, the sale happens the day the enquiry arrives. 61% of every membership Bandra sells is sold on the same day, and the median lead buys on the day it enquires. Everything after that is a small, slow tail.

Third, the studio’s biggest channel is its weakest. Website and online sources deliver 3,714 leads — 47% of the file — and convert 8.9% of them at ₹4,120 of lifetime value. Calls, messages and referrals together deliver 1,920 leads and convert 23.9% of them at ₹9,031.

The single sentence version

This is not a studio that cannot attract people. It is a studio that attracts 7,822 of them, converts the ones who walk in or ring up, and then leaves 2,120 of the rest sitting in a file whose average entry is 603 days old.

The trial is the gate

A lead who has taken a class converts at 12 times the rate of a lead who has not. Nothing else in the file is close.

3,493 leads completed a trial and 26.1% of them became members. Of the 4,329 who did not, 2.19% converted — 95 people out of 4,329. Mean lifetime value is ₹11,888 against ₹24 — effectively nothing.

This single fact reorganises everything else in this report. Cost per lead, source quality and channel mix all matter, but they matter because they change how many trials get booked. A channel that produces a hundred leads and twenty trials is worth more than one that produces three hundred leads and twenty trials, and the studio currently reports only the first number.

Speed decides it

61% of wins happen on day zero. The studio is a same-day counter with an unmeasured response time.

Of the 951 Bandra leads that converted and carry a usable date pair, 577 — 61% — bought on the same day they enquired. The next day accounts for 6.3%, and the whole of the first week for 74.3%. The median lead buys on the day it enquires.

The tail is small but instructive. The 194 wins that took a month or longer are worth ₹42,525 on average, against ₹38,832 for same-day wins. Patience is rewarded, but only 20.4% of the studio’s business comes that way. The practical conclusion is not that slow leads are valuable; it is that a lead who has not converted within the first week is almost certainly gone.

What this means for the front desk

Every enquiry that arrives and is answered the next morning has already lost most of its value. The studio’s conversion rate is therefore a description of how fast it answers, not of how persuasive it is — and unlike persuasion, answering speed is entirely within its control.

Where the leads come from

Volume and value sit in different channels, and the gap between them is the studio’s largest untapped gain.

Bandra records six channels. Website & online is dominant at 3,714 leads — 47% of the file — and converts at 8.9%. Calls & messages brings 881 leads at 25.3%, and Referrals & word of mouth brings 1,039 at 22.7%.

The named sources inside those channels sharpen the picture further. Website is the largest source in the file at 3,090 leads and the weakest of the major sources at 8.1%. Incoming sms is the strongest at 32.0% on 50 leads, and Incoming call carries the highest lifetime value at ₹20,201. 2,120 open leads. A mean age of 603 days. 1,836 of them more than six months old.

Trial completion has risen sharply this year. Conversion has not followed it, and the volume is falling.

Read as a cohort — every lead grouped by the month it arrived — the 2026 file shows a studio getting better at the middle of its funnel and no better at the end of it. Trial completion has moved from 37.9% in January to 54.5% in September, a rise of 17 points. Conversion has moved from 9.2% to 6.3%, down 3 points.

Recommendations

Twelve actions, ordered by the value each releases
01

Nothing matters more than the trial — treat it as the only target

Studio Manager + CRM

Reasoning3,493 of 7,822 Bandra leads completed a trial and 1006 of them became members. Of the 4,329 who never took a trial, 95 ever bought anything. A completed trial converts at 26.1%; a lead without one converts at 2.19%. Mean lifetime value is ₹11,888 against ₹24.

Expected impactEvery hour spent on a lead who has not booked a class is worth a fraction of the same hour spent getting that class booked. The studio’s single operational target should be the number of trials booked this week, and every other lead metric should be read as a consequence of it.

02

Answer on the day, because the sale is made on the day

Front Desk + CRM

Reasoning61% of every membership Bandra sells is sold the same day the enquiry arrives — 577 of 951 wins. The median wait from enquiry to purchase is 0 days. Wins that took a month or more are 20% of the volume and are worth ₹42,525 on average.

Expected impactThis is the most decisive number in the file. The studio is not running a nurture funnel; it is running a same-day counter. Response time is therefore not a service standard — it is the conversion rate, delayed. A same-day callback on every new enquiry is the highest-yield process change available and it costs nothing.

03

Fix the first-response date, then set a target against it

CRM + Front Desk

ReasoningMedian first response is 1 to 3 days across the team, and roughly a fifth of the records carry a follow-up date that precedes the enquiry itself — the field is being back-filled rather than logged at the time.

Expected impactA metric that can be written after the fact is not a metric. Until the first-response field is captured automatically, the studio cannot tell a two-hour call-back from a two-day one, and every conversation about lead handling rests on recollection rather than record.

04

Move the acquisition mix towards calls, referrals and walk-ins

Marketing

ReasoningWebsite and online sources produce 3,714 leads — 47% of everything Bandra attracts — at 8.9% conversion and ₹4,120 of lifetime value. Calls and messages produce 881 at 25.3% and ₹10,185; referrals produce 1,039 at 22.7% and ₹8,052.

Expected impactA referral lead is worth 2.5 times a website lead and converts 2.8 times as often. The studio does not need more leads; it needs the leads that already know someone. A visible referral reward, published at the point of enquiry, is the cheapest mix change in this report.

05

Decide what hosted classes are for

Programming + Marketing

ReasoningHosted classes generate 3,090 leads, and 25% of them complete a trial — the highest trial rate of any source in the file. But only 8.1% become members, at ₹3,955 of lifetime value.

Expected impactHosted classes are an excellent trial machine and a poor acquisition channel. Either the studio accepts them as community marketing and stops counting them as a growth channel, or it changes what happens at the end of a hosted class — a booked next class rather than a card left on a table.

06

Publish conversion by associate and manage the range

Studio Manager

ReasoningConversion ranges from 9.7% for Deesha Changwani to 20.4% for Nadiya Shaikh on the same product list at the same prices. Mean lifetime value per lead ranges from ₹2,655 to ₹6,804.

Expected impactThe strongest closer is not necessarily the one holding the biggest book, which is exactly why the range is worth publishing. A monthly table, without names attached, moves the middle of the distribution; pairing the top performer with the largest in-box moves the top.

07

Close the open file honestly

CRM

Reasoning2,120 Bandra leads are still marked open and their mean age is 603 days. 1,836 of them are more than six months old, and 1,076 are sitting at the same stage — pricing and schedule shared, decision never recorded.

Expected impactAn open lead that is two years old is not a pipeline; it is a missing status. A single afternoon of honest disposition — contactable, interested, or closed — would turn 2,120 rows into a short, real list and make every conversion figure the studio reports trustworthy again.

08

Work the fresh open leads and stop counting the rest

CRM + Front Desk

ReasoningOnly 56 open leads are less than thirty days old. Those are the ones the studio can still win, and they are a list one person could clear in a week.

Expected impactSeparating the file into a live queue and an archive is a five-minute change with a disproportionate payoff: it makes the daily follow-up task finite, and a finite task gets done. The archive should still be contacted at renewal season, but it should not sit in the working list.

09

Target the trial at the class people already name

Programming + Marketing

ReasoningBarre 57 is named on 5,508 leads and PowerCycle on 2,014. Between them they account for 96% of all leads with a recorded preference.

Expected impactThe studio records what each lead wants and then books the trial into whatever slot is free. Matching the first class to the stated preference is a scheduling decision, not a marketing spend, and it removes the commonest reason a first impression fails.

10

Stop buying outdoor acquisition until it can be measured

Marketing

ReasoningOutdoor classes produce 45 leads at 2% trial completion, 0.0% conversion and ₹0 of lifetime value — the weakest result in the file on every measure.

Expected impactEvery channel in this report should be held to the same two numbers: what it costs and what a lead from it is worth over a lifetime. Outdoor is currently the only line where those two are not compared, and on the evidence it is the first budget the studio should question.

11

Give the small, high-value sources more room

Marketing

ReasoningIncoming calls produce 120 leads at 27.5% conversion and ₹20,201 of lifetime value. Influencer sign-ups produce 129 leads at 14.0% and ₹10,451.

Expected impactNeither is a volume channel and neither needs to be. Both return more per lead than anything the studio spends against at scale, and both are currently incidental rather than funded. A published phone number and two more influencer partnerships are cheap experiments with a proven tail.

12

Report leads weekly, not annually

Management

ReasoningThe studio’s lead reporting is retrospective. A weekly page carrying four numbers — leads created, trials booked, trials completed and memberships sold — would have shown the September weakness in its first week rather than in this report.

Expected impactLeads are the earliest signal the studio has: they move a full quarter before attendance does. A short weekly discipline on those four numbers turns this report from an explanation into an early warning, and it needs no new system — only a standing appointment to read it.

Sources and method

The CRM lead master holds 25,315 records across all centres, of which 7,822 belong to Bandra and are used throughout. A lead is counted once, at creation, and its outcome is the status the record carries at snapshot; recent cohorts are therefore understated for conversion and overstated for open. Channel, source, associate and class preference are the studio’s own fields, used as recorded.
Response time is the interval between the lead’s creation and the first of four follow-up dates. The four comment fields are populated on every record but are largely administrative placeholders, so contact quality cannot be measured from this file at all.
Lifetime value is the value the CRM carries against the lead, not an independently reconstructed figure; it is used for ranking channels against each other, which is the only comparison it supports. Cash figures are as recorded at snapshot on 18 October 2026 and are not contribution margin.

reports.title: Supreme HQ, Bandra — Member Behaviour and Patterns
reports.intro: Member Behaviour and Patterns  ·  September 2026 Supreme HQ, Bandra — how members actually behave 394 members trained at Bandra in September 2026, 1,404 times between them. This report is about the shape of that behaviour rather than its size: when members come, how long they leave between visits, how often they buy, how far they get before they stop, and which of those patterns the studio can actually change. The headline is that most of what looks like churn is a single early step that nobody owns. Check-in ledger · 39,777 attended entries · 4,840 members September 2026 · 394 members · 1,404 visits · 3.56 each September 2025 · 305 members · 1,476 visits · 4.84 each Snapshot 18 October 2026
reports.html:
Start here

Half the members came once. The most frequent tenth delivered two fifths of the attendance. And almost all of the loss happens at a single step.

The studio’s members are morning people. 249 of 394 members do most of their training before noon, against 129 who come in the evening. The busiest hours of September were 11:00 (265 check-ins) and 09:00 (252), and the busiest day was Tuesday.

They come in clusters, not on a schedule. The median gap between a member’s visits is 1 day, and 85% of every gap on record is a week or less. Bandra members do not train twice a week; they come three days running and then not for a fortnight.

And the loss is concentrated in one step. Across 1,785 first-timers, 40.5% make a second visit, and of those 70% go on to a third. 59.5 points of the cohort are lost at the first repeat visit — and then the curve reverses: from the second visit onward, each next visit is more likely than the last.

The single sentence version

This studio does not leak members steadily. It loses most of them once, in their first fortnight, and it never sees the moment coming because it measures attendance rather than the interval between visits.

When members come

Mornings carry the studio. The evening block carries a smaller group of equally committed members, on the same timetable.

September recorded 1,404 check-ins across 394 members. Read by the hour, the pattern is emphatic: 252 check-ins at 09:00 and 265 at 11:00, against 226 at 18:00 and 223 at 19:00. Read by the member rather than the visit, the same picture hardens — 249 of the 394 members have their modal hour before noon, 129 after five, and 16 in between.

The two groups are the same customers at different times of day. Morning-first members averaged 3.72 visits in the month, evening-first members 3.57 and midday members 1.06 — within a few per cent of each other. The evening block is not a lesser audience; it is simply a smaller one, and it is scheduled as though it were the larger.

How often members come

The median interval between two visits by the same person is one day. Nobody designs a timetable for that.

Look at the interval between one visit and the next for the same member, across the whole ledger, and the studio’s real rhythm appears — and it is not weekly. 17,662 of 34,937 consecutive-visit gaps are a day or less, and 85% are within a week. The median gap is 1 day.

Members come in bursts: several sessions close together, then a pause. That pattern is usually read as inconsistency, and it is usually treated with plans and targets that assume a weekly rhythm the members have never had. The commercially important consequence is different and more useful: a pause is normal. The studio cannot tell a healthy gap from a lapse by the gap alone, and should not try — what matters is whether the member comes back, and how fast.

How often members buy

Purchases cluster even more tightly than visits, and the buying decision is made in the first fortnight.

Across every repeat purchase on record, the median gap between two purchases by the same person is 14 days, and 64% of all repeat purchases happen within thirty days. The gaps then thin sharply: 668 run to two months, 315 to three, and 409 run to six months.

Two thirds of Bandra’s buyers have made exactly one purchase ever — 53.5% of the file. For the rest, buying is a monthly act, not an annual one. That leads to a simple operational conclusion: the renewal offer belongs in the first fortnight of a membership, while the member is at peak usage, rather than in its final week when the visits have already stopped.

The rhythm of the month

The desk is busiest in the hour after the morning classes, and the month is busiest in its first fortnight.

Sales are recorded at the moment they are taken, and the timestamps are unambiguous. The single busiest hour of the 2026 trading year is 12:00 — after the 09:00 and 11:00 classes come out, not before them. The busiest weekday for sales is Saturday and the quietest Sunday. Within the month there are two peaks, around the 11th to the 14th and again at the very end, with a clear trough in the last full week.

Put together, the studio’s own transaction log says where a sales push should sit: at the desk, at noon, in the first half of the month. That is not a marketing insight so much as a scheduling one — but it is the difference between an offer that arrives during a member’s routine and one that arrives after it.

The shape of the base

52% of members came once. The most frequent tenth delivered 42% of the attendance.

September’s 394 members do not distribute like a membership base. 205 of them came exactly once — 52% of the base — while the 39 members who came most often delivered 42% of every seat filled. The middle of the distribution is thinner than the extremes.

This is the arithmetic behind the studio’s headline numbers. A base that is 52% single-visit will show reasonable member counts and weak attendance in the same month, every month, until the single-visit group is either converted or discounted. The 39 regulars are not a bonus; they are the studio.

Attendance is a product of two numbers — how many members and how often they come — and the studio manages the first far more actively than the second. Across the last eighteen months, visits per member have run between 2.29 and 4.92. September 2025 sat at 4.84; September 2026 came in at 3.56.

The member count over the same period has generally risen, which is why the fall in frequency has been easy to miss: more members, each coming less often, produces a member-count headline that looks healthy and an attendance number that is flat to falling. Routine and variety

Members who do one thing repeatedly stay longer than members who do many things once — and the best outcome is both.

38% of September’s members used more than one format in the month, and 94 members (24% of the base) made three or more visits to a single format. The two behaviours are not in tension. A member who has a home format and also explores is the member who is still here next September; a member who does neither is the member who came once.

The check-in ledger already records each member’s modal hour and favourite format. Nothing in the studio currently uses either one to hold a slot, invite a member into the next format, or notice when a routine breaks. That is the cheapest personalisation available to Bandra, and it needs no new system.

Own the second visit as a product, not an outcome

Studio Manager + Front Desk

ReasoningAcross 1,785 Bandra first-timers, 40.5% reach a second visit and 28.5% reach a third. The first repeat visit is the gate: 59.5 points of the cohort never come back a second time.

Expected impactBut the gate is also the only one. Of the members who return once, 70% return again; of those, 82% come back a fourth time. Bandra does not lose members steadily — it loses them once, at the first repeat visit, and almost everyone who clears that step stays. An owned, dated, booked second class is the whole of the retention strategy.

02

Build the timetable around mornings, because that is when members come

Programming + Studio Manager

Reasoning249 of the 394 members who trained in September do most of their training before noon, against 129 who come in the evening and 16 at midday. Morning-first members averaged 3.72 visits in the month and evening-first members 3.57.

Expected impactThe studio schedules its evenings as heavily as its mornings on the assumption that working members come after work. The member data says its audience is a morning audience that also uses the evening. Rebalancing a third of the evening timetable into the 09:00 and 11:00 blocks follows the members rather than fighting them.

03

Stop expecting members to come on a schedule, and design for the cluster

Studio Manager

ReasoningThe median gap between a member’s visits is 1 day. 85% of every gap on record is a week or less, and more than half are within a day. Members do not train twice a week on a rhythm; they come in bursts.

Expected impactA studio that believes in the rhythm sells rigid plans and measures consistency. A studio that understands the cluster sells flexibility and measures return rate. The same member behaviour reads as churn under a rhythm and as normal under a cluster — and the second reading is the correct one.

04

Sell the next purchase at the point of the last one

Front Desk + CRM

ReasoningThe median gap between a member’s purchases is 14 days, and 64% of all repeat purchases happen inside a month. 668 gaps run to two months and 409 run to half a year.

Expected impactBuying behaviour at this studio is monthly, which means the renewal conversation belongs in the first fortnight of the membership rather than in its final week. A renewal offered when a member is at peak usage renews far more often than one offered after the visits have already stopped.

05

Treat the single-visit member as the studio’s core problem

Front Desk + CRM

Reasoning205 of 394 members — 52% — came exactly once in September. At the other end, the 39 most frequent members delivered 42% of every seat the studio filled.

Expected impactA base where a third of the people come once and a tenth deliver a third of the attendance is not a membership base; it is a trial pool with a small permanent core. The economics of the studio are decided at the join between those two groups, and that join is the second visit.

06

Give every member a preferred slot, and keep it

Programming + CRM

Reasoning94 members — 24% of the base — made three or more visits to the same format in September, and 38% of members used two or more formats in the month.

Expected impactA member with a standing slot is a member with a habit, and a habit is far harder to break than a preference. The studio can see each member’s modal hour and favourite format from its own check-in ledger; nothing currently uses either to hold the slot for them.

07

Read the monthly frequency number as the studio’s headline metric

Management

ReasoningVisits per member have run between 2.29 and 4.92 across the last eighteen months, and September 2026’s 3.56 is the lowest full month in the series. Attendance, revenue and member counts are all downstream of it.

Expected impactThis is the only number on the studio’s dashboard that moves before the others and explains all of them. A base that grows while frequency falls will produce flat attendance and a falling revenue-per-member, which is precisely what the last quarter has looked like.

08

Put the members who came once into a fourteen-day sequence

CRM + Front Desk

Reasoning205 members came once in September and have not been seen since. The relative-second-visit data says most of them will not come back on their own, and the ones who do will arrive within a week of their first class.

Expected impactA fortnight is the entire window. A message on day two, a booked class on day five and a call on day ten will recover more of this group than any offer made to the whole base, because it arrives while the first class is still the member’s most recent memory of the studio.

09

Schedule the money, not just the classes

Front Desk + Finance

ReasoningSales peak at 12:00 — after the morning classes rather than before them — and 18% of the year’s September-to-date sales fall in the first week of the month against 31% in the last week.

Expected impactThe desk needs staffing, offers and renewal conversations where the money already is. Placing the sales push in the hour after the morning block, and in the first fortnight of the month, works with the members’ own behaviour rather than against it.

10

Give the quiet regular a reason to come back this week

CRM + Studio Manager

ReasoningThe members who come most often carry the studio, and they are the ones whose absence costs the most. A member who drops from ten visits a month to five is invisible in every headline attendance figure and is worth more than a new joiner.

Expected impactA weekly list of members whose visits have fallen by half against their own four-week average — not against the studio’s — is the highest-yield retention tool available, and it needs no new data collection. The studio measures everyone against the same target; habit should be measured against the member’s own baseline.

11

Measure the base by how often it comes, not only by how many it is

Management

ReasoningSeptember had 394 members and 1,404 visits. September 2025 had fewer members and more visits. A member-count headline reads as growth in a month whose attendance fell.

Expected impactThe base and its frequency need to be reported side by side in every monthly pack, because they can move in opposite directions and one of them flatters. The studio has spent this year growing the numerator of a ratio whose denominator was shrinking.

12

Keep the two habits that are working

Studio Manager

Reasoning38% of September’s members used more than one format, and 24% made three or more visits to a single format. Both behaviours are associated with longer membership lives than either alone.

Expected impactVariety and routine are not opposites here; they are the two halves of a member who stays. Every programming and induction decision should be judged by whether it encourages one of them, and the studio should report both monthly.

Sources and method

Behaviour is read from the Day End Part 4 check-in ledger, filtered to Supreme HQ, Bandra (39,777 attended entries across 877 days). A member is counted in a month if they checked in at least once; revenue-weighted activity is deliberately excluded so that one large purchase cannot make a quiet member look active.
Buying behaviour comes from the raw sales export, filtered to Bandra and to records with a valid sale date. Consecutive-visit and consecutive-purchase gaps are computed within each person, so each member contributes at most one observation per pair.
The visit-number curve uses every member whose first visit was in the year to August 2025, so that every cohort member has had at least twelve months to accumulate visits. Members who joined later are excluded rather than truncated.
Cash figures are as recorded at snapshot on 18 October 2026 and are gross, not contribution margin.

reports.intro: Performance Review  ·  September 2026 Supreme HQ, Bandra September brought the studio its highest September intake on record. It also produced its weakest conversion, and the second-weakest retention. This edition reads September against three years of history, adds the check-in ledger, the lead register and the sales ledger to the member file, tests eight candidate explanations against the data — and finds three that hold, one of which was not visible in any of the earlier numbers. 143 new clients 150,895 check-ins · 25,315 leads · 25,044 sales Equal-observation methodology

Start here

September is an outlier inside a steady year — not the start of a decline

The most important fact about September 2026 is what it is not. It is not the month the studio's fundamentals broke. Over the twelve months to September, Bandra's second-visit rate held at 29.2% versus 29.1% the year before, and the revenue generated per new client within 90 days rose to ₹2,431 from ₹2,259 — the second consecutive annual improvement. Volume across the trailing twelve months was effectively flat, at 1,439 clients against 1,475.

Year-to-date the picture is equally reassuring on the metric that matters most. Across January to September 2026, the share of new clients who returned for a second class was 39.1%, against 39.2% in 2025 and 37.4% in 2024. Whatever went wrong in September, it did not go wrong for the year.

One qualification belongs here rather than in a footnote, because it cuts across every retention figure in this report and is quantified in full later. Roughly a third of what the studio records as a "second visit" is the pre-paid second half of a Newcomers 2 For 1 intro pack — a class the client has already bought and is simply using up. These year-level rates are therefore the right measure for spotting change over time, because the same distortion runs through all three years, but they overstate the absolute level of genuine repeat demand. Where a true return rate is quoted below, the pre-paid visits have been removed.

What September did was concentrate a set of already-visible weaknesses into a single month, in a way that is now measurable and therefore fixable. This edition adds three further sources — the full 150,895-row check-in ledger, the 25,315-record lead register and the 25,044-record sales ledger — which together make it possible to say not just what happened in September but where it happened and who it happened to.

The short version of what those sources add. September's revenue was carried almost entirely by members the studio already had, which is why the month looked normal in the accounts while its future quietly thinned. Nearly six in ten of the month's failed leads were simply never reached, or asked for more time. The studio's second-visit rate is overstated by the intro pack, which pre-pays the second visit. And the single most consequential change at Bandra this year was not in marketing or pricing at all: it was who was standing at the front of the room.

Two true statements that look like they contradict each other

The sales ledger shows September 2026 taking ₹15,29,410 across 213 transactions — down only 2.3% on September 2025 and, in isolation, an unremarkable month. The member cohort file shows the 143 clients acquired in September generating ₹2,35,543 of cash so far, against ₹9,47,989 for the 99 clients acquired a year earlier.

Both are correct, and the distance between them is the single most useful thing in this review. 87.5% of September's revenue came from members the studio already had, and only 12.5% from anyone new. September's till looked healthy because the existing base kept paying. September's future got visibly thinner.

This is why the two figures should be read together rather than instead of one another. A flat top line is genuinely good news — it means the studio is not losing its existing members, which is the harder and more valuable half of the business. But it also means the ledger was masking the acquisition problem completely. Had this month's new-client shortfall been read only through the till, it would have been invisible.

The September picture

Acquisition succeeded. Follow-through did not.

Volume was the month's clear success. At 143 new clients, September 2026 was the studio's strongest September in the dataset — 44% above 2025 and 22% above the trailing monthly average — and Bandra's share of group-wide intake climbed to 36.6% from 27.7% a year earlier. What went well

Four things September got right — and should keep

Conversion speed was the fastest on record

Clients who converted in September did so in a median of 3 days, against an all-time Bandra median of 8. Two-thirds converted within a week. When intent was present, the studio captured it quickly and without friction — a genuine operational strength worth protecting.

Those who did convert bought larger packages

The median first purchase among September converters was ₹16,734 — the highest of any month in the past year, against ₹14,222 in August and ₹9,639 in July. Half bought the Studio 12-Class Package, compared with 23% historically. September's converters were fewer but higher-intent and higher-value.

Paid-entry clients performed exactly to norm

Clients who paid for their first visit converted at 25.0%, against a 25.8% historical rate, at ₹9,824 of value each. This is the studio's smallest entry channel at just 4 clients — and its most reliable. It is a case for considered expansion, not retreat.

Barre 57 held the line, and several trainers excelled

Barre 57 delivered 59% of the month's revenue and the studio's best format-level conversion at 13.3%. Individually, Anmol Sharma placed 6 of 14 new clients into a second class — a 42.9% follow-through rate that is the strongest individual result in the studio this month, and proof the model works when it is executed well.

Root cause

Five explanations tested against the data

Eight candidate explanations were examined — the ones that are obvious, and the ones that are easy to miss. Four do not survive contact with the numbers. Three do, and they turn out to be linked.

Confirmed — first order

The teaching roster turned over

Five trainers who carried a large share of client-facing classes in September 2025 — Cauveri Vikrant, Karanvir Bhatia, Karan Bhatia, Simonelle De Vitre and Mrigakshi Jaiswal — took 65% fewer classes in September 2026 (1,112 down to 394). The group that absorbed that load rose from 221 classes to 545, up 147%. Their clients are worth materially different amounts: ₹8,701 per new client for the departing group against ₹6,617 for the incoming one.

The largest single change at Bandra between the two Septembers was not demand, price or marketing. It was an unmeasured swap of the people who deliver the first class — the one moment that determines whether a client ever comes back.
Confirmed

One trainer held 23% of the month's intake, and none returned

Reshma Sharma received 33 of September's 143 new clients — 23% of the entire month. Not one attended a second class, anywhere in the network. Trial-for-trial, her clients converted at 0 of 18 against 9 of 61 (14.8%) for the rest of the studio.

Her all-time record is unremarkable rather than poor, which is the point: a zero month can happen to anyone, and the studio should never have a quarter of its acquisition resting on one person with no second look.
Confirmed

The lead pipeline stopped closing

Leads rose 40% year-on-year while wins fell 48%. Win rate collapsed from 17.0% to 6.3%. Of the 2,572 leads that closed as lost with a reason recorded, 38.4% were simply unreachable and 20.1% were postponements; only 2.1% cited price.

Interest is not the constraint. Follow-up is. This is the cheapest problem in the review to fix and the one with the shortest payback.
Ruled out

Ganesh Chaturthi disrupted the month

Ganesh Chaturthi fell on 14 September, with visarjan on the 25th — and Bandra sits on the procession route. But splitting September into festival phases, the pre-festival window converted at 7.1%, no better than the festival window at 6.2%. A festival suppresses a studio for ten days; it does not suppress the week before it. The weakness was already present on 1 September.

September 2024 shows the same test with the opposite result: pre-festival 46.7%, festival 24.5%. The pattern is not stable enough to be causal.
Ruled out

Demand fell across the market

On the identical matched basis, Kwality House converted at 13.8% and Kenkere House at 30.8% while Bandra sat at 12.5%. Kenkere's conversion actually improved year-on-year. Bandra's intake also rose 44%, which is not the signature of a soft market.

The dip is studio-specific, not market-wide.
Ruled out

Volume overloaded the team

Across 21 months at Bandra, monthly volume correlates with conversion rate at just +0.08 and with second-visit rate at -0.03. Some of the studio's strongest months were also among its highest-volume.

High intake is not, by itself, a cause of poor conversion. This matters: it points away from staffing and effort.
Confirmed

Intake mix shifted toward low-intent entry

Hosted-class share against second-visit rate correlates at -0.64 across 21 months — the strongest relationship in the data. Free-entry share at -0.57, weekend share at -0.46. September combined a 23.8% hosted share with a 52.4% weekend share, and 18.2% free entry.

This is a mix problem, not a demand or effort problem — and mix is directly controllable.
Ruled out

Capacity or attendance was down

Bandra ran 251 classes in September 2026 against 266 a year earlier, filled 1,404 seats against 1,476, at 44.0% capacity utilisation against 43.0%. Average class size was 5.6 against 5.5.

The studio ran very close to a normal schedule with a normal audience. Footfall fell only 4.9% — there was no shortage of people in the room.
Contributing

Follow-up execution on the 12–13 September weekend

The month's single largest intake block — 30 clients in two days, 21% of the month, against a daily average of 4.8 — produced zero conversions and ₹709 of revenue. Thirteen were attendees of one partner event, none of whom returned.

It accounts for 85% of the month's conversion gap on 43% of the cohort. A specific, datable, avoidable trigger.

The finding that was hiding

Who was teaching, and what happened to the clients they received

The most consequential change at Bandra between September 2025 and September 2026 was not in marketing, pricing or demand. It was who was standing at the front of the room.

Five trainers who carried a large share of the studio's client-facing load in 2025 — Cauveri Vikrant, Karanvir Bhatia, Karan Bhatia, Simonelle De Vitre and Mrigakshi Jaiswal — between them took 1,112 classes in September 2025 and 394 in September 2026, a fall of 65%. The newer group that absorbed that load — Reshma Sharma, Pranjali Jain, Anmol Sharma and Rohan Dahima — rose from 221 classes to 545, an increase of 147%. Total studio bookings fell 24.8% over the same period.

This matters because the trainers who left or reduced their hours were not interchangeable with those who replaced them on the measure that drives the business. Across their full history, the five departing trainers brought in new clients who were worth ₹8,701 on average. The four who replaced them have brought in clients worth ₹6,617 — a difference of roughly ₹2,084 per new client.

It is worth being precise about what is and is not being claimed. This is not an argument that the incoming trainers are worse teachers. It is the narrower, harder observation that a studio's first-class experience is delivered by a person, that not all first classes are equally effective at producing a second one, and that Bandra conducted a large, unmeasured swap of exactly that variable in the twelve months to September.

Reshma Sharma took 33 of the month's 143 new clients — 23.1% of the entire month's intake, more than double any other trainer. Every one of those 33 clients attended exactly one class. On lifetime value per client she ranks 2 of 10 among trainers with 150 or more clients, at ₹7,310. A zero month can happen to anyone.

What cannot be waved away is the arithmetic of the concentration. To test whether the result was genuinely meaningful or simply an unlucky sequence, her clients can be compared to the rest of the studio on the narrowest possible basis — trial-class clients only, the same entry type, the same month:

  • Trial clients taught by Reshma Sharma: 18 clients, 0 converted.
  • Trial clients taught by everyone else: 61 clients, 9 converted — 14.8%.

At the rest of the studio's rate, 33 clients would have been expected to yield 3.6 new members. If that probability is taken as the baseline, the chance of drawing zero conversions from 33 consecutive clients purely by luck is about 2.2% — roughly one in fifty. On the sharper return-visit measure the arithmetic is starker still: had her 33 clients returned at the 21.8% rate the rest of the studio achieved, that would be seven people; the probability of seeing none by chance is well under one in a thousand.

The genuinely useful point is not about one trainer's month. It is that a single instructor held 23.1% of the studio's new-client intake with no hedge. Whatever the cause of a zero month — personal circumstances, an off-period, a mismatch between her coaching style and the trial population, a scheduling accident — the studio had no second look at those clients. A quarter of the month's acquisition pipeline passed through one pair of hands and was never reviewed by anyone else.

That concentration is itself the finding, and it is directly fixable: cap any one trainer's share of first visits, and route every trial client to a second touchpoint — a different class format, a different trainer, a follow-up call — before the relationship is allowed to end.

The pipeline problem

More interest than ever, and less of it being closed

If September's conversion problem were a demand problem, the lead log would show fewer people walking in. It shows the opposite. The intro pack, and an honest second-visit rate

The cheapest class the studio sells, and what it actually buys

The second-visit rate is overstated, and the intro pack is why

Of the 24 September clients who attended a second class, 11 were simply redeeming the second half of a pre-paid Studio Newcomers 2 For 1 pack they had already bought. That visit cost the studio a class and required no decision from the client. Only 13 of the 24 were genuine, unprompted returns.

This is the user-facing arithmetic: the headline September second-visit rate of 16.8% falls to 9.1% once pre-paid redemptions are removed. Put differently: 46% of what looked like returning demand was a class someone had already paid for. Across the trailing eleven months the same effect runs through roughly 37% of all recorded second visits.

The reason this is not a technicality is that the 2-for-1 is not a neutral product. It is priced at ₹1,855 for two classes — ₹927 a class, against ₹1,738 for a single class and ₹1,278 per class inside the 12-class package. It is the cheapest class the studio sells, by a wide margin. That is a defensible acquisition price. The question is what it acquires.

The numbers are uncomfortable. Of 807 Bandra members who have bought the intro pack, only 37.5% have ever bought anything else. The median 2-for-1 entrant's total lifetime spend at Bandra is ₹1,838 — which is to say, the intro pack and almost nothing after it. The honest interpretation is that the 2-for-1 is doing one job well and another badly. As a low-friction trial it works — it gets people through the door at a price they will pay, which is exactly what it is for. But it is not producing members, and it is distorting the studio's own retention metrics while it does so. It flatters the second-visit rate in every month it operates, which means the studio’s true rate of genuine repeat demand is lower than any of its dashboards show. A 2-for-1 buyer who returns for class two has not yet made a single repeat-purchase decision.

The correction matters most when the same adjustment is applied to both sides of the comparison, which is the only way to read it fairly. On the canonical matched window — first visits in the opening thirteen days of the month — the ledger says 12.9% of September clients returned against 36.9% on the trailing eleven-month norm, a gap of 24.1 points. Strip out the pre-paid redemptions from both sides and the figures become 8.6% against 23.2% — a gap of 14.6 points.

Both readings matter, and they point in different directions. The absolute level is worse than it looks: September's genuine second-visit rate of 8.6% is just over a third of the 23.2% the studio actually achieves once the coupon effect is removed from its own history. But the fall is less severe than the headline suggests, because the pre-paid distortion flatters the baseline more than it flatters September (37.3% of nested returns are pre-paid historically against 33.3% in September). The honest summary is that the studio's normal retention is genuinely strong — 23.2% real returns is a good number for any boutique studio — and September delivered less than half of it.

The practical consequence is a definitional one that the studio should adopt immediately: a client who bought a two-class intro pack becomes a genuine returning client on their third visit, not their second. On that definition Bandra's numbers look different, and more honest, across every month in the dataset.

What the studio did not see

Three second-order effects, and one structural risk

Some obvious explanations are worth stating plainly, even where they turn out to be wrong, because ruling them out is what makes the remaining explanation credible — and because two of them turn out to be right.

The studio ran a normal schedule at normal class sizes

Bandra held 266 classes in September 2025 and 251 in September 2026. Seats offered fell 7.0%, from 3,433 to 3,191. Capacity utilisation was 43.0% last year and 44.0% this year; average class size was 5.5 then and 5.6 now. September 2026 was not a month of empty rooms or a thinned-out timetable. It was very close to September 2025 in operational shape.

This is genuinely useful, because it removes the largest alternative explanation. The month did not fail for want of capacity or for want of attendance — 1,404 people attended classes in September 2026 against 1,476 a year earlier, a fall of only 4.9%. Footfall was essentially intact.

The same footfall is being spread across more people, and that is the hidden cost

Here is the second-order effect that is genuinely easy to miss. Attendance held roughly flat while the number of distinct members attending it rose. Bandra drew 1,404 attended visits from 394 members in September 2026, against 1,476 from 305 members in September 2025. Visits per attending member fell from 4.84 to 3.56 — and 3.38 for September on the full-month basis, the lowest monthly figure of 2026.

The studio looks equally busy at the same level of effort. Underneath, the same number of bodies is composed of more, shallower relationships. That is a quieter and more consequential shift than a visible drop in attendance, and it points at the same underlying issue as the conversion shortfall: the studio is getting people in the door and not keeping them in the room.

Late cancellations have been genuinely fixed

One notable operational improvement deserves credit, and it is easy to overlook because it is a number that got better. The no-show and late-cancellation rate fell from 30.8% in September 2025 to 12.5% in September 2026. That is a structural improvement rather than noise — the rate has stayed near 12% every month since the change — and it returns real bookable capacity to the schedule without a single extra class being added. Against a background of harder acquisition, this is a genuine operational win and it should be protected.

On the fully matured slice of the September cohort — the 70 clients who visited between 1 and 13 September, each observed for at least 28 days — the trailing norm predicts 10.0 thirty-day conversions. 5 occurred.

The distribution of that shortfall is the most important finding in this review. The first eleven days of September performed essentially to norm — 5 conversions against 5.7 expected, a gap of less than one client across 40 people. The entire remaining shortfall, 85% of it, sits in the weekend of 12–13 September, which absorbed 30 clients in two days and produced none of the month's conversions.

Scaled across all 143 September clients, the gap amounts to roughly 10 clients who would normally have become members. Measured in first-purchase revenue over the next few months that is about ₹1,07,516; measured across the lifetime of those relationships, at the studio's observed conversion economics, it is approximately ₹2,89,753. Separately, the 12 missing second visits in the matured slice represent around 7 further conversions — about ₹2,01,998 of lifetime value that is still recoverable through follow-up rather than acquisition.

That decomposition uses the ledger's own visit counts, and the intro pack touches it too. On the same matched window the genuine second-visit rate is 8.6% rather than the published 12.9%, because 3 of the nine returns were pre-paid 2-for-1 redemptions. Setting that alongside a baseline adjusted the same way — 23.2% genuine returns historically — the true gap on the matured slice is about 10.2 returns rather than 11.6, worth roughly ₹1,78,027 of recoverable lifetime value. The correction narrows the distance from normal but sharpens the level: September's genuine return rate is barely a third of the studio's own.

Seen this way, September is not a story of systemic failure, and it is certainly not a story about the studio's everyday operation. Ordinary trading in the first eleven days was sound. Two days of concentrated, complimentary, event-driven intake absorbed a fifth of the month's clients, returned none of them, and accounted for effectively the whole of the month's value loss. That is a schedulable, preventable event — which is why it is the first recommendation in this report rather than an acceptance of decline.
